topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Comparing durations
topic.description: Use comparative language for time: quicker, slower, earlier, later
evidence: Compare two events and say which was quicker/slower
Use 'earlier' and 'later' correctly to describe daily events
Solve practical problems like 'Who finished first?'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} finishes their dinner before a sibling, can they tell you who finished earlier — and which one was quicker?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to compare how long events take and when they happen, using quicker/slower (duration) and earlier/later (position in time). The deep hurdle is separating DURATION from other cues: young children judge 'how long' by distance covered, speed, or which event stopped last (the Piagetian time–speed–distance confusion), so the faster or further event is wrongly thought to take longer. Taught by comparing real timed events and talking them through.
bestPractices: Compare two real events side by side — races, sand-timers, classroom tasks — and name which was quicker/slower
Use a common start so 'who finished first' is a fair judge of quicker
Explicitly separate 'finished later' (position) from 'took longer' (duration) with same-start and different-start examples
Anchor earlier/later to the daily timeline
Use the vocabulary in live commentary on real events
keyRepresentations: Two events on a shared start-line / common timeline
Sand-timers or a visible stopwatch
A race with a common start
The daily timeline for earlier/later
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by distance or speed — the faster/further one 'took longer' (or slower means less time)
Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took more time', ignoring the start
Confuses earlier/later (position) with quicker/slower (duration)
Ties 'a long time' to how much happened rather than elapsed time

learn.summary: Young children (ages 4-6) learn to compare how long events take (duration: quicker/slower) and when they happen (position in time: earlier/later). The core hurdle is separating DURATION from distance, speed, which event stopped last, or how much happened during an event — the classic time-speed-distance confusion, where a faster, further-travelling, or busier event is wrongly judged to take longer. Teaching uses real timed events compared side by side, with explicit talk separating 'finished later' from 'took longer'.

activities.title: Watch duration grow from a shared start
feedback: If the learner picks the faster or further event as 'took longer', replay both from a shared start with visible timers and point to which bar is shorter: that one took less time.
If the learner says the slow-motion walk took less time, run the same path at normal and slow speed side by side so they watch the slower bar come out longer.

If the learner judges 'a long time' by how much happened, compare a busy event that finishes quickly against a calm event that runs on, and read the timers: a lot can happen in a short time, so duration is what the clock shows, not how much went on.
When the learner correctly reads the shorter bar as quicker and explains that the slow trip took more time, confirm that duration is about elapsed time, not speed, distance, or how much happened.
activities.rationale: Making duration visible as a growing bar from a shared start, independent of speed and distance, targets the specific confusion where faster/further/busier is read as longer. A same-path slow-motion comparison isolates speed from duration; a different-start mode isolates start time from finishing order; a busy-short vs calm-long comparison isolates amount-of-activity from elapsed time. The growing-bar, slow-motion toggle and different-start mode are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: Young children characteristically confuse duration with speed and distance (time–speed–distance confusion), judging that a faster or further-travelling object took more time; a coordinated concept of duration develops gradually.

NCETM Year 1 assesses comparative duration with a walking-to-school scenario designed to separate duration from speed: 'On Tuesday I walk more slowly — does my journey take more or less time?' and 'On Wednesday it takes 8 minutes — on which day do I walk quickest/slowest?', with pupils explaining their reasoning.
learnerActions: Start two events at the same moment and watch a visible timer or growing duration-bar under each until it stops
Name which event was quicker — the one with the shorter bar/time — and say how you know
Use a slower-speed toggle to make a walker go along the SAME path at a slower walking speed, while the timer runs in real time, and watch its duration-bar grow longer than before
Say out loud: 'slower over the same way means MORE time'
Switch to a mode where the two events start at DIFFERENT times, and decide whether 'finished last' really means 'took longest'
activities.intendedInsight: Duration can be seen directly — how long something takes on the clock — separately from how fast it goes, how far it travels, or how much happens during it. Going slower over the same route takes MORE time, not less. Finishing last is not the same as taking longest when starts differ.

activities.title: Race and time real events with a common start
feedback: If the learner says whoever stopped last 'took the most time' when starts differed, point out that one started earlier; ask how they could make it a fair race (same start).
With a shared start, confirm that the one who finished first really was quicker because both began together.
If the learner uses distance ('he went further') to decide duration, set up a same-distance comparison with timers so only the time differs.

Use the walk-to-school times both ways: with 10 minutes on Monday, 12 minutes on Tuesday and 8 minutes on Wednesday, Wednesday (8 minutes, the least time) was the quickest walk and Tuesday (12 minutes, the most time) was the slowest. Compare the actual times each way.
activities.rationale: Comparing real timed events with a common start gives a concrete, fair basis for 'quicker', while a contrasting different-start case makes start time visible as something that matters. Sand-timers of 30 seconds and 1 minute and a shared colouring start are concrete examples supporting authentic comparison.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'compare, describe and solve practical problems for ... time [for example, quicker, slower, earlier, later]'.

NCETM Year 1 assesses comparative duration with a walking-to-school scenario designed to separate duration from speed: 'On Tuesday I walk more slowly — does my journey take more or less time?' and 'On Wednesday it takes 8 minutes — on which day do I walk quickest/slowest?', with pupils explaining their reasoning.
learnerActions: Compare two real timed events side by side — a race, two sand-timers (e.g. 30 seconds and 1 minute), or two classroom colouring tasks
Begin both from a common start so 'who finished first' is a fair judge of who was quicker
Name which event was quicker and which was slower, and explain how you know
Set up a case where the two events start at different times and discuss why 'finished first' no longer settles who was quicker
activities.intendedInsight: When two events share a start, finishing first means quicker. When starts differ, you must consider when each began — finishing order alone does not tell you who took longer.

activities.title: Talk through events using quicker/slower/earlier/later
feedback: If the learner answers 'who was quicker?' with 'he came later', gently separate the two: later tells us WHERE on the day; quicker tells us HOW LONG on a timer.
If the learner argues the further runner took longer, ask how they could check with a timer over the same distance.

For the two-cars case (red goes further, green still moving after red stops), help the learner see that 'went further' does not mean 'took more time'. If both cars started together, green, which was still moving after red stopped, took more time. If the start times are different or unknown, 'still moving after' does not settle it, so check when each started or time both from the same start.

Note: confusing earlier/later with quicker/slower is developmentally expected and tends to self-correct with maturation — separate the two in their own contexts rather than treating it as an error to drill.
activities.rationale: Authentic commentary and a questioner who probes reasoning invite genuine use of the vocabulary and surface the distance/speed-equals-duration intuition so it can be addressed in words. The two-cars probe additionally separates finishing-order and distance from elapsed time. Anchoring earlier/later to the daily timeline keeps position distinct from duration. A live commentator/questioner is one illustrative format; discussion can be led by any adult.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'compare, describe and solve practical problems for ... time [for example, quicker, slower, earlier, later]'.
learnerActions: Give live commentary on a race or on the day's events, saying who or what was quicker/slower and what happened earlier/later
Answer a questioner who asks 'Who was quicker? How do you know?' and respond to the challenge 'but he ran further — does further mean longer?'

Reason about a case like two cars where the red car goes further but the green car was still moving after the red one stopped. If both started at the same moment, the green car took more time even though it went less far. If you don't know when each started, decide what else you need to know.
Explain the difference between finishing EARLIER (where on the day) and being QUICKER (how long it took)
Place daily events (breakfast, lunch, home-time) on a timeline to anchor earlier/later
activities.intendedInsight: Quicker/slower describe how long something took (duration on a timer); earlier/later describe where an event sits on the day's timeline (position). These are different ideas and should be used in their own contexts. Going further is not the same as having taken more time. Still moving after another stopped means more time only if both started together.

activities.title: Decide quicker/slower and order by duration
feedback: If the learner picks 'less time' for the slower same-route walk, revisit a side-by-side timed comparison so they see the slower trip's time is larger.

For a walk-to-school item (for example Monday 10 minutes, Tuesday 12 minutes, Wednesday 8 minutes), the 8-minute day took the least time, so it was the quickest, and the 12-minute day took the most time, so it was the slowest. Check that the learner compares the actual times.
Confirm correct orderings by duration and ask the learner to say why the chosen event was quicker.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and ordering tasks check whether comparative time language is used correctly and make duration-vs-speed a natural discriminating item. These formats mainly check and consolidate recognition and ordering; they do not themselves require the learner to produce and justify a comparison in their own words, which open commentary and hands-on timing do call for.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 assesses comparative duration with a walking-to-school scenario designed to separate duration from speed: 'On Tuesday I walk more slowly — does my journey take more or less time?' and 'On Wednesday it takes 8 minutes — on which day do I walk quickest/slowest?', with pupils explaining their reasoning.
Year 1 pupils should 'compare, describe and solve practical problems for ... time [for example, quicker, slower, earlier, later]'.
learnerActions: Given two timer pictures, choose which event was quicker
Put several events in order by how long they took
Match daily events onto a timeline using earlier/later
Answer a 'walk more slowly over the same route — more or less time?' question and explain your reasoning
activities.intendedInsight: You can judge and compare durations from timer readings, and the slower trip over the same route takes MORE time — a check on the speed-equals-less-time intuition.

constraints: A static two-timer picture with tap-to-reveal can label quicker/slower but, being static, cannot animate duration growing independently of speed; use it as a scaffold, not as the moment that dislodges the confusion.
Selected-response/ordering tasks consolidate and check correct use of time language but do not require the learner to construct and justify a comparison in their own words.

Comparing duration is not primarily a spatial task, so a 3D representation offers little over clear timed comparisons here; this is a scoping note, not a claim that any medium is incapable of teaching it.
Treat earlier/later vs quicker/slower confusion as developmentally expected and largely self-correcting; separate the two in their own contexts rather than reteaching it as a misconception.
Keep comparisons fair: use a common start when finishing order is meant to show who was quicker, and only introduce different-start cases deliberately to teach that start time matters.

The Piaget time-speed-distance source is marked verified:false in the row; the developmental claim is retained verbatim as background context only and should not be treated as freshly confirmed or as efficacy evidence.
NCETM item arithmetic checked: 8 minutes < 10 minutes, so the 8-minute (Wednesday) day is quickest and the slower Tuesday walk is slowest; this matches the row's stated correct answer.

The row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that a static image 'can't' dislodge the confusion; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog ratings do not establish such universal claims.
Coverage for the 'a long time = how much happened' misconception (present in the original set) is included in the summary and Activity 1.
The original two-cars probe (red further, green still moving after red stopped) has been restored to the conversation activity as a distinct concrete discriminator.
The growing duration-bar, slow-motion toggle, and different-start mode are preserved as optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only valid teaching method.

probeDeeper: 'You walked more slowly today — so did it take MORE time or LESS time? Why?' (duration vs speed)
'Two cars race. The red one goes further, but the green one was still moving after red stopped. Which took more time? How could we be sure?' (separates distance from duration)
'What is the difference between finishing EARLIER and being QUICKER?'
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies the shorter timer as quicker; reasons that walking more slowly over the same route takes MORE time, and that 8 minutes < 10 minutes so Wednesday was quickest; says the child who finished first (same start) was quicker. Uses quicker/slower for duration and earlier/later for position, correctly.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges duration by speed or distance, not elapsed time — the faster/further event 'took longer', or slower means less time
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare same-distance events with a shared start and a visible timer so duration is separated from speed; narrate 'slower over the same way means MORE time'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the walking item says walking more slowly takes LESS time, or picks the faster/further event as the one that took longer

errorPatterns.pattern: Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring when each started
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a shared start line so finishing order really does show duration; then contrast a different-start case explicitly so the child sees start time matters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When start times differ, says whoever stopped last 'took the most time' without considering the start

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses earlier/later (position in time) with quicker/slower (duration)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach or treat this as a misconception — the earlier/later vs quicker/slower distinction self-corrects with maturation. Instead, separate the two in their own contexts — earlier/later = WHERE on the day's timeline, quicker/slower = HOW LONG on a timer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'who was quicker?' with 'he came later', or uses 'earlier' to mean 'slower'

responseLevels.gap: Judges 'how long' by distance/speed or by who stopped last; uses quicker/slower/earlier/later interchangeably or by non-time cues.
responseLevels.full: Uses quicker/slower for duration and earlier/later for position correctly, reasons that slower over the same distance takes more time, and separates duration from speed/distance and from finishing position, transferring to a new comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Uses quicker/slower correctly for clear same-start comparisons, but is caught by the speed-vs-duration confound (slower = less time) or confuses earlier/later with quicker/slower.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set up real comparisons and listen for correct USE: (1) Two sand-timers (30 seconds and 1 minute) started together: 'Which one is quicker? How do you know?' (2) 'On Monday my walk to school takes 10 minutes. On Tuesday I walk more slowly — does Tuesday's walk take more or less time? On Wednesday it takes 8 minutes — which day was I quickest?' (3) 'We both started colouring at the same time and I finished first — who was quicker?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'walk more slowly — more or less time?' item is the classic duration-vs-speed probe: a child with the time–speed–distance confusion says slower means less time, or judges by distance; the same-start colouring item checks 'finished first = quicker' with no start-time confound.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Ordering Events in Time
topic.description: Sequence events in chronological order using language such as before, after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon, evening
evidence: Order three daily events using 'first', 'next', 'last'
Use 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' correctly
Describe an event as happening in the 'morning' or 'afternoon'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to describe what happened this morning in order, can they use words like "first", "then", "after that" — putting breakfast before leaving for school?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to order events in time and to USE relational time language — first/next/last, before/after, the deictic terms today/yesterday/tomorrow, and morning/afternoon/evening. The hard part is the deictic terms, whose referent shifts with 'now' (tomorrow becomes today the next day), and the relational before/after. It is learned by talking through the daily routine and retelling sequences, not by definitions.
bestPractices: Anchor in the child's own daily routine and shared class events, with a visual timeline of the day
Use the words in live narration ('first we…, next we…, after lunch we…') and in story retelling
Tie yesterday/today/tomorrow to concrete markers — what we DID and what we WILL do
Teach by modelling and eliciting USE, never by asking children to define the words
Revisit the terms daily so the shifting deictic meaning is rehearsed in context
keyRepresentations: A visual daily-timeline / sequence strip of routine events
Story-sequencing picture cards
A yesterday–today–tomorrow three-day strip with a moveable 'today' marker
commonMisconceptions: Swaps yesterday and tomorrow (both used loosely for 'a day that isn't today')
Reverses before/after, or uses 'next' for the last thing
Ties morning/afternoon to particular activities rather than the time of day
Sequences by salience (the most exciting event first) rather than chronology

learn.summary: For children aged 4-6, learning to order events in time and USE relational time language — first/next/last, before/after, the deictic terms today/yesterday/tomorrow, and morning/afternoon/evening. The hardest parts are the deictic terms (whose referent shifts as 'now' moves — tomorrow becomes today the next day) and the relational before/after. These are learned by talking through the daily routine, retelling sequences and stories, and anchoring words to concrete remembered and anticipated events — not by asking children to define words. Research describes deictic time words as acquired slowly and partially, so early slips are best treated as developmental rather than errors to drill.

activities.title: Order the day and slide the 'today' marker
feedback: If events are ordered by interest rather than time (e.g. the exciting event first), re-walk the actual order along the picture sequence, asking 'what happened right before this? what happened right after this?' — ground it in the concrete routine or story rather than labelling it wrong.

If the child swaps yesterday and tomorrow, anchor each word to a concrete event ('yesterday we had PE; tomorrow we go to the park') rather than correcting with a rule; these slips are expected at this age and resolve with exposure.
When the child narrates correctly, echo their words back to confirm: 'Yes — first wake up, next breakfast, last bed.'
After sliding the marker, prompt: 'Now that today has moved, what is yesterday? What is tomorrow?' so the shifting reference is rehearsed.
activities.rationale: A moveable 'today' marker makes the shifting deictic reference visible: sliding it and watching 'yesterday'/'tomorrow' re-label is a concrete way to rehearse the system that children otherwise learn implicitly from discourse. Drag-to-order supports sequencing as a natural action, whether for the daily routine or for retelling a story. The curriculum lists this vocabulary for Year 1, and the deictic shift is the documented difficulty.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.

Deictic time words are acquired slowly and partially: 3-year-olds perform at chance on deictic status, treating 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as merely 'non-present' before distinguishing past from future (so the two are readily interchanged); adult-like deictic status and sequential order emerge together and reach majority mastery before age 6 (status ~5;4, order ~5;8), while temporal remoteness develops independently and later, after age 7 (~7;3). Children PRODUCE these words around age 3 but do not comprehend them adult-like for several years, and they learn status/order from natural-language cues (tense, discourse) rather than explicit teaching — supporting treating early slips as developmental, not as errors to drill.
learnerActions: Put pictures of the day's events — wake up, breakfast, school, bed — into chronological order.
Narrate the ordered sequence aloud using 'first… next… last' (e.g. 'first we wake up, next we have breakfast, last we go to bed').
The same drag-to-order can be used with story-sequencing picture cards: retell a familiar story in order, not only the daily routine, narrating it with first/next/last.

On a scrolling strip of consecutive days with a moveable 'today' marker (e.g. Tuesday–Wednesday–Thursday), start with 'today' on the MIDDLE day so both neighbours are visible, and say what happened yesterday (the day before) and what will happen tomorrow (the day after).

Slide the view forward one day, keeping 'today' on the middle slot: the day that was 'tomorrow' is now 'today', the day that was 'today' is now 'yesterday', the oldest day slides off and a new day comes into view ahead, so all three relative labels stay represented and keep re-pointing.
activities.intendedInsight: Yesterday and tomorrow are not interchangeable words for 'a day that isn't today' — they name a definite place relative to where 'now' sits, and they re-point as 'today' moves. Sequencing follows real chronology, not how exciting an event is.

activities.title: Talk through your day with a character
feedback: Keep exchanges short and concrete for a 4-6 year old; follow the child's lead rather than quizzing.

If the child ties 'morning' or 'afternoon' to a particular activity rather than the time of day, gently re-anchor to the time of day itself — afternoon is the part of the day after the middle of the day (midday) until evening — and point out that several different activities can happen in the afternoon, so the label tracks the time, not one event.
Model correct use in the reply rather than correcting: if the child says 'yesterday' meaning tomorrow, respond with the concrete anchor ('oh, the park is tomorrow — the day that is coming!').
activities.rationale: Because the objective is USING the vocabulary in context, an in-role conversational partner is a proposed way to elicit authentic spoken production, which recognition or scoring alone does not capture. Research suggests children learn much about these terms from cues in everyday conversation, so modelling them in natural talk is a sensible approach.
sourceClaims: Deictic time words are acquired slowly and partially: 3-year-olds perform at chance on deictic status, treating 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as merely 'non-present' before distinguishing past from future (so the two are readily interchanged); adult-like deictic status and sequential order emerge together and reach majority mastery before age 6 (status ~5;4, order ~5;8), while temporal remoteness develops independently and later, after age 7 (~7;3). Children PRODUCE these words around age 3 but do not comprehend them adult-like for several years, and they learn status/order from natural-language cues (tense, discourse) rather than explicit teaching — supporting treating early slips as developmental, not as errors to drill.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly character recount their own day in simple, concrete terms.
Tell the character what you did first and next in your own day.
Answer what you did yesterday and what you will do tomorrow, tied to real events you remember or expect.
Use 'morning' and 'afternoon' to say when something happened.
activities.intendedInsight: Time words are tools for talking about real, remembered and anticipated events — using them in authentic exchange is the goal, not reciting definitions.

activities.title: Name the parts of the day (naming scaffold)
feedback: If a child fixes 'afternoon' to a single activity, show the same part of the day with different activities so the label tracks the time, not the event.
Use this as a naming warm-up, then move to ordering and live narration where the child must actually use the words.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal timeline names the parts of the day usefully, but it does not let the child sequence events or experience the deictic shift, so it serves as a vocabulary scaffold rather than the full objective.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.
learnerActions: Tap parts of a daily-timeline picture to reveal labels — morning, afternoon, evening.
Match everyday activities to the time of day they usually happen.
Say when each shown activity happens using 'morning', 'afternoon' or 'evening'.
activities.intendedInsight: The day has named parts tied to the time of day, not to which single activity happens.

activities.title: Order a novel set of events
feedback: The shuffled-pictures item reveals a child who sequences by interest rather than time: re-walk the real order along the timeline.
The fresh-anchor deictic item separates a child who holds the system (answers shift correctly around 'today') from one who uses yesterday/tomorrow interchangeably for 'not-today'.
Probe gently if needed: 'You said tomorrow — is that the day that is coming, or the day that has finished?'; 'What do you do BEFORE you come to school, and what do you do AFTER?'
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching can be scored, but a fixed task cannot assess spontaneous USE in live context, which is the crux — so keep listening for correct use in the flow of talk. Using a novel set and a fresh anchor is intended to test transfer rather than a rehearsed routine.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.
learnerActions: Order a set of shuffled routine pictures (e.g. wake up, school, bed) into chronological order.
Narrate them with 'first', 'next', 'last' in true time order.
Match given activities to morning/afternoon/evening.

Answer a fresh-anchor deictic question, e.g. 'If today is Friday, is tomorrow a school day or the weekend?' (use this only where Saturday is a non-school weekend day for the child; otherwise choose days that match the child's own school week).
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that sequencing and deictic reasoning transfer to a new, unrehearsed set of events and a fresh 'today' anchor.

constraints: Teach by modelling and eliciting USE; never ask a 4-6 year old to define a time word.
Anchor in the child's own daily routine, shared class events and familiar stories, and revisit the terms daily so the shifting deictic meaning is rehearsed in context.
Tie yesterday/today/tomorrow to concrete markers — what we DID and what we WILL do.
Anchor morning/afternoon/evening to the time of day, not to a single activity: afternoon is the time after midday until evening, and many different activities can happen then.

Treat early slips (swapping yesterday/tomorrow, reversing before/after, sequencing by salience) as developmental, expected and self-correcting with age and exposure — not as errors to drill or confront with a rule.
The static part-of-day timeline is a naming scaffold only: it does not let the child sequence or experience the deictic shift, so do not rely on it for the full objective.
Scored ordering/matching tasks cannot assess spontaneous spoken use in live context; combine them with listening for correct use in conversation.
Keep conversational exchanges short, concrete and child-led for this age range.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row. Sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Story-sequencing picture cards / story retelling, present in the original keyRepresentations and bestPractices, was missing from the prior candidate and has been restored as a drag-to-order alternative in the first activity.

The original rated a 3D artefact 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim has been dropped — ordering events in time is not inherently spatial, but the source does not establish that 3D can never help, so no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted either way.

The original framed the conversational artefact as 'strong' and the 2D interactive as the single ideal; this rewrite preserves both as distinct activities with different purposes (deictic-shift visualisation vs authentic spoken use) rather than ranking them.

One source (Harner 1975) is marked verified:false in the row and is cited via later reviews; its specific finding (children confuse yesterday with tomorrow but not with today) is not used as an exact sourceClaim and is noted as supporting background only.

The mastery ages cited (status ~5;4, order ~5;8, remoteness ~7;3) sit partly inside and above this 4-6 band; teachers should expect many children in range to be mid-acquisition, consistent with the 'treat slips as developmental' guidance.

The prior candidate's morning/afternoon re-anchor example tied 'afternoon' to lunch and conflated midday with afternoon; it is corrected to anchor on the time of day with varied activities. The consecutive-day strip keeps 'today' on the middle slot and scrolls so yesterday and tomorrow stay represented before and after sliding.

probeDeeper: 'You said tomorrow — is that the day that is coming, or the day that has finished?'
'If today is Friday, is tomorrow a school day or the weekend?' (deictic reasoning on a fresh anchor)
'What do you do BEFORE you come to school — and what do you do AFTER?'
assess.correctAnswer: Uses 'morning' and 'after' correctly while narrating; correctly names yesterday as the day before and tomorrow as the day after today; orders the three events and narrates them with first/next/last in true chronological order.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach or correct this with a rule — deictic time words (yesterday/today/tomorrow) resolve with age and exposure, so treat slips as expected, not as an error. Instead, anchor each word to a concrete event ('yesterday we had PE; tomorrow we go to the park') and use them daily in routine talk.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'yesterday' when meaning tomorrow (or the reverse), or uses them at random

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not confront this as an error or drill a rule — sequence ordering firms up with maturation. Instead, narrate the real sequence while pointing along a timeline strip ('this comes BEFORE this') and rehearse it in context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the flow of talk about the day and week, listen for correct USE (never ask the child to define a word): (1) 'Tell me what you do in the morning, and what you do after that.' (3) Show three shuffled routine pictures (wake up, school, bed): 'Put these in order and tell me what happens first, next and last.'

topic.description: Recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months, and years

topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} what day it is today, what day yesterday was, and what month we're in, can they answer all three — and tell you how many months are in a year?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to name and use the days of the week and months of the year in order, and to grasp their NESTED, CYCLIC structure — 7 days in a week, weeks and 12 months in a year, all of which repeat. The main risk is rote recitation (the 'days song') without functional understanding: knowing the chant but unable to say what comes after Thursday or to read a calendar.
bestPractices: Run a daily calendar routine ('today is…, yesterday was…, tomorrow will be…')
Connect days/months to real cyclic events — the weekend, birthdays, seasons
Build the nesting explicitly (days → weeks → months → year) with a visual calendar
Ask 'what comes after / before X' out of song order, and go backwards, to build random access
Use months via real dates and events, not recitation alone
keyRepresentations: A wall calendar / month grid
A days-of-the-week wheel showing the cycle
A year strip divided into 12 months
Birthday and seasonal anchors on the calendar
commonMisconceptions: Recites the sequence but can't start from the middle ('what's after Wednesday?') without restarting
Cannot work backwards through the days/months
Doesn't grasp nesting — treats week, month, year as unrelated, or a year as vaguely 'a long time'
Treats the cycle as linear — nothing comes after Sunday or December

learn.summary: Children learn to name and use the days of the week and months of the year in order, and to grasp their nested, cyclic structure — 7 days in a week, about four weeks plus a few days in a month, and 12 months in a year, all of which repeat. The main risk is rote recitation (the 'days song') without functional understanding: knowing the chant but unable to say what comes after Thursday or to read a calendar. Guidance targets functional use (random access in both directions), the cycle (the week/year comes round again), and the nesting (days inside weeks and inside months, months inside a year; weeks do not fit into months exactly, so a week can run across two months).

activities.title: The looping days wheel: jump in anywhere, go both ways
feedback: If the child sings the whole sequence to answer 'what's after Thursday', gently pause them and point to Thursday on the wheel: 'Start right here — which day sits next to it?'
If the child says 'there's no day after Sunday', turn the wheel past Sunday to show it loops back to Monday: 'Look — the week comes round again.'
When the child names the day before a given day without restarting, confirm that they can now jump in anywhere and go either way.
activities.rationale: A visible loop makes the cyclic structure something the child can see rather than only a rule stated to them, and tapping any day supports random access in both directions. Random access and the cycle are the intended functional objectives beyond recitation; the curriculum source supports using day-of-week language, and the NCETM calendar task frames functional use over reciting, though neither prescribes this particular wheel. Showing the loop is one concrete way to make the cycle visible — a page-turning calendar or verbal routine can serve the same end.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months and years'.
learnerActions: Spin or turn a days-of-the-week wheel and watch it roll past Sunday straight back to Monday, so the week never 'ends' — it comes round again.
Tap or point to any day (e.g. Wednesday) and name 'the day after' without singing from Sunday.
Answer 'what's after / before X' questions starting from a day in the middle, moving both forwards and backwards.
Optional: tapping a day lights up the day after and the day before so the child can check their answer against the wheel.
activities.intendedInsight: The days form a repeating cycle you can enter at any point and travel in either direction — not a one-way song that must restart from the beginning.

activities.title: Zoom from a day to the year: nesting made visible
feedback: If the child says a week is longer than a month, show the month-grid holding several week-rows: 'Count the full weeks inside this month — there are four whole weeks, and most months have a few days left over.'
If the child can't locate a birthday month in the year, point to the year-strip: 'Find the start of the year — now count along to your birthday month.'
When the child explains that a month contains several weeks, affirm the nesting idea explicitly.
activities.rationale: Building the containment visually (days in a week-row, weeks in a month-grid, months along a year-strip) supports the ordering/length comparisons the sources probe, and anchors the nesting that recitation alone does not convey.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 assesses relative length of time-units with 'circle the times which are shorter than 1 week' from the options 1 year, 1 day, 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 month — targeting the nesting/ordering of days, weeks, months, years.
learnerActions: Start from a single day, then pull back to see the week-row it sits in, then the month-grid that contains that day (noticing that some week-rows run into the month before or after), then the whole year-strip of 12 months.
Place a birthday or seasonal event and say which month it is in and whether that is near the start, middle or end of the year.
Order time-units by length and answer 'which is longer, a week or a month?', explaining how you know.
Optional: a nested visual (day inside week-row inside month-grid inside year-strip) the child can move between to see the containment.
activities.intendedInsight: Days sit inside weeks and inside months, and months sit inside a year — the units are related, not separate. A month holds about four weeks plus a few extra days (weeks do not fit into months exactly), so a month is longer than a week.

activities.title: Count across the calendar: dates and weekdays together
feedback: If the child guesses without counting, have them put a finger on the starting date and step one square per day aloud.
If the child gives only the date or only the day, prompt for the other: 'And what day of the week is that one?'
When the child names both the date and the weekday after counting on, confirm they are now using the calendar, not the chant.
activities.rationale: Counting across real dates and naming both date and weekday mirrors the NCETM functional (not rote) calendar task directly, catching whether the child can use the day/date structure.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery assessment probes functional (not rote) date knowledge with a January-calendar task — pupils use day-of-week clues to identify dates ('she is visiting her aunty on a Tuesday; this is [ ] January', 'three days after the party she is going swimming') — requiring counting across the calendar rather than reciting.
Year 1 pupils should 'recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months and years'.
learnerActions: Using a real January-style month calendar, start from a given date and weekday (e.g. 'your party is on Saturday the 6th').
Count on across the calendar: 'Three days after the party you go swimming — point to that date and tell me the day.'
Use day-of-week clues to find a date (e.g. 'she visits her aunty on the first Tuesday after the party — which date is that?').
Name both the date and the weekday for the day you land on.
activities.intendedInsight: A calendar lets you count across dates and link each date to its weekday, which is using the structure rather than reciting it.

activities.title: Daily calendar talk: functional use in conversation
feedback: If the child restarts the song to answer, redirect to today's day: 'Start from today — what comes after it?'
If the child names a month but not whether it is near the start or end of the year, prompt a position ('is that near the beginning of the year or the end?').
Praise functional answers that reference real events, e.g. linking the weekend or a birthday to a day or month.
activities.rationale: Spoken daily calendar talk elicits functional use at any starting point and in context. A visual can show the loop and the nesting directly while speech states them, so pairing conversation with a calendar or wheel is sensible; conversation complements the visual structure work, and neither medium is asserted as superior or required alone.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months and years'.
learnerActions: Join a short daily routine: 'Today is…, yesterday was…, tomorrow will be…'.
Answer an in-role question such as 'what day will it be after the weekend?' or 'what month is your birthday in?'.
Reason aloud from a known day to an upcoming one, connecting days and months to real events (the weekend, birthdays, seasons).
Match months to seasons when a season is mentioned, using the seasons where the child lives (the months for each season differ between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres).
activities.intendedInsight: Days and months are tools for talking about real time — when things happened and will happen — not just a list to chant.

activities.title: Order and choose: sequencing and comparison questions
feedback: For 'what comes after Thursday?', if the child restarts the song, point to Thursday in the ordered set and ask for the next item only.
For the shorter-than-a-week task, if a longer unit (a month or a year) is chosen, remind them a week holds several days and a month holds several weeks.
Confirm correct selections and ask the child to say how they decided, to surface reasoning.
activities.rationale: Selection and ordering items make the sequence and relative-length knowledge visible and align with the NCETM 'shorter than 1 week' task; as recognition/selection tasks they check knowledge rather than elicit independent construction, so pair them with the spoken and calendar tasks above.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 assesses relative length of time-units with 'circle the times which are shorter than 1 week' from the options 1 year, 1 day, 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 month — targeting the nesting/ordering of days, weeks, months, years.
learnerActions: Put the days (or the months) in order.
Answer 'what comes after Thursday?' style questions, including ones that start from the middle of the sequence.
Circle or select the time-units shorter than a week from a set such as 1 year, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute, 1 month.
Match months to the seasons they fall in where the child lives (the months for each season differ between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres).
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering and length-comparison tasks check that the child knows sequence and relative size, not just the chant.

constraints: The core objective is functional use — random access in both directions, grasping the cycle and the nesting — not rote recitation of the days/months chant.

A static calendar with tap-to-reveal facts names the parts but does not itself show the loop or let the child count across dates; use it as a naming scaffold and pair it with a cyclic representation and a counting task.

Selection/ordering/multiple-choice items check knowledge of sequence and relative length but do not elicit independent spoken or calendar use; include at least one task where the child counts on a real calendar and names the date and weekday aloud.

The looping wheel and nested zoom are concrete ways to make cycle and nesting visible; they are suggested affordances, not the only valid medium — a page-turning calendar, year-strip, or verbal routine can serve the same purposes.

Rote recitation without random access, weak nesting, and a linear (non-cyclic) view are largely developmental for this age: build the structure visually and with daily practice rather than re-drilling the chant or confronting the child with a rule.

The original quiz designNotes listed the 'shorter than a week' options as '1 day, 1 hour, 1 month, 1 year', omitting '1 minute' present in the verified source claim; the activity restores the full source set (1 year, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute, 1 month).

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches the second hand go all the way round a clock, can they count that as one minute — and estimate roughly how many minutes their favourite TV show lasts?

pedagogy.summary: Children begin to MEASURE elapsed time with tools — sand timers, stopwatches, counting seconds — to time real activities, and to record the result in simple units ('about 2 minutes'). The step is procedural and embodied: start the tool as the activity starts, stop it as it ends, read off the duration. The conceptual underpinning (from the prerequisite) is that duration is how long something lasts, independent of speed; children also begin to meet 1 minute = 60 seconds.
bestPractices: Time real, meaningful activities (how long to write your name, to tidy up) with a visible tool
Model starting and stopping the tool exactly AT the start and end of the event
Use sand timers first — duration is visible as the sand falls — before digital stopwatches
Introduce 1 minute = 60 seconds by counting seconds until a one-minute sand timer empties
Record informally ('about 2 minutes', 'a bit more than a minute') rather than demanding precision
keyRepresentations: Sand timers of known durations (1 minute, 3 minutes)
A stopwatch or large seconds display
A number line / counting track of seconds
A one-minute timer paired with a count to 60
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by speed or by how much happened, not elapsed time (carried from comparing durations)
Starts or stops the tool out of step with the event
Reads the number currently showing as the duration, ignoring where timing started
Thinks 'a minute' and '60 seconds' are different amounts

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 5-6) learn to MEASURE elapsed time using tools — sand timers, stopwatches, counting seconds — to time real activities and record results in simple units ('about 2 minutes'). The core skill is procedural and embodied: start the tool exactly as the event begins, stop it exactly as it ends, then read off the duration. The conceptual underpinnings are that duration is how long something lasts from start to finish, measured with a tool rather than judged by how fast, effortful or busy the activity felt, and that 1 minute = 60 seconds, which is a genuine conceptual step because 60 is not a base-ten grouping.

activities.title: Time a real activity with start and stop aligned to the event
feedback: If the start or stop lagged or led the real event, replay it: count '3-2-1 start' together and stop on the final action. Focus on tightening the timing action; a timing slip on its own does not mean the child misunderstands duration.

If the spoken duration tracks effort ('it took ages because it was hard') but disagrees with the tool, bring attention back to the reading on the tool, then time two equally-effortful tasks that take different amounts of time so duration separates from effort.
Prompt reflection: 'You said about a minute — how do you know it was about a minute?' and 'If you had started the timer a bit late, would your answer be too much or too little?'
activities.rationale: Statutory Year 1 Measurement content asks pupils to measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes and seconds. Research locates the difficulty in measuring/recording elapsed duration rather than naming units (noting that the supporting figures come from Years 3-4 studies), so practising the act of timing a real event — starting and stopping in step — targets the hardest strand directly.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'measure and begin to record the following: ... time (hours, minutes, seconds)' (statutory Measurement content).

Duration is the weakest strand of children's time understanding in Years 3-4 (only ~50% full understanding vs ~60% for measurement/succession), and measuring duration using the hands of a clock is specifically among the challenging items — so measuring/recording elapsed time, not naming units, is where difficulty concentrates.
learnerActions: Pick a short, real activity to time (e.g. writing your name five times, tidying a small tray, building a block tower).

Choose the right tool: for an open-ended duration use a stopwatch or a seconds count/large seconds display; a fixed one-minute sand timer is best for checking whether something takes about a minute or comparing against its known span.
Hold the visible timing tool ready.
Count '3-2-1 start' and start the tool at the exact moment the activity begins.
Stop the tool the instant the activity finishes (on the last action).
Read off and say the duration in simple terms, e.g. 'about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds', 'a bit more than a minute'.
Repeat with a second activity and compare which took longer.
activities.intendedInsight: 'How long' is a quantity you can capture with a tool by aligning start and stop with the event, not a feeling guessed from how fast or how effortful the activity was.

activities.title: Build 1 minute = 60 seconds by counting a one-minute timer
feedback: If the child treats 'a minute' and '60 seconds' as different amounts, pair the two directly: count seconds in time with a seconds display while the one-minute timer empties so the same span is both about '60 seconds' and 'one minute'.
Probe: 'The sand timer ran out — how many seconds was that?' to check the minute is linked to a count of 60.
Note that a sand timer and a stopwatch may not match exactly depending on the tools; treat 'would it agree?' as something to observe and discuss, not a guaranteed result.
activities.rationale: Children reason about time with discrete whole-number thinking and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so 1 minute = 60 seconds is a real conceptual step. Counting seconds against a one-minute timer makes the grouping concrete rather than asserted.
sourceClaims: Children treat time with discrete whole-number reasoning and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the relationship 1 minute = 60 seconds is a genuine conceptual step rather than an obvious fact.
learnerActions: Turn over a one-minute sand timer and count the seconds aloud (or follow a seconds display) until the sand runs out.

Notice that the count reaches about 60 as the minute ends, provided each number is paced to one second (e.g. by following a seconds display); young children counting freely often go faster and reach a higher number.
Say the relationship: 'one minute is the same as 60 seconds.'
Check with a second tool: 'If we used the stopwatch instead, would it agree?'
activities.intendedInsight: A minute and 60 seconds are the same amount of time, not two different amounts — the 60-grouping is something you can experience by counting it out.

activities.title: Compare two durations and read a growing span, not the end number
feedback: If the child reports the final stopwatch reading as 'how long it took' on a watch that was not started from zero, always zero or note the start, and use a bar that grows from the start so duration is its length.

OPTIONAL supportive display: a bar that grows as time passes and a 60-second ring that fills once per minute can make the accruing duration and the minute visible; a mis-timed start would visibly shorten or stretch the bar. These are illustrative aids, not required equipment — sand timers and a counting track of seconds work too.
activities.rationale: A common error is reading the number currently showing as the duration while ignoring where timing began. Representing duration as an accruing length from the start addresses this by making the span itself the thing being measured. This representation is a research-informed design proposal; no source directly tests it.
learnerActions: Time two different activities and record each duration ('about 20 seconds', 'about a minute').
Represent each duration as a length — e.g. a bar that grows FROM the start, or line up the two timings side by side.
Decide which activity took longer by comparing the lengths.
If using a stopwatch, note or zero the start first, so the duration is the span covered, not whichever number happens to show at the end.
activities.intendedInsight: Duration is the amount of time that elapsed between start and stop — represented as a length that grows from the start — not simply the number currently displayed.

constraints: This is a procedural, embodied skill: assess by WATCHING the child start and stop the tool with the event, not by asking them to recite the procedure or a fact. Reciting '1 minute = 60 seconds' is not by itself evidence they can measure.

Prefer sand timers first — duration is visible as the sand falls — before digital stopwatches; a fixed sand timer and a stopwatch give different experiences (checking a known span vs capturing an open-ended duration) and can be compared, with neither being universally necessary.
Record informally ('about 2 minutes', 'a bit more than a minute') rather than demanding precision at this age.

A recognition/ordering quiz (reading a stopwatch value, ordering activities by length) can check whether a child reads a duration, but does not elicit the act of measuring — starting and stopping in step with an event — which is the main objective.
A static labelled timer image can name the parts of a tool but does not let the child time an event or watch a duration accrue; use it as a scaffold, not as the performance itself.
Sand timers and stopwatches are concrete tools; a screen bar/ring display is one optional representation of the same idea, not a replacement for timing a real activity.

The representational crux is that the two hands mean different things and move together: at half past, the minute hand points to 6 and the hour hand sits HALFWAY between two numbers, and the time is 'half past the last number the hour hand has passed'. Establish o'clock first (minute hand on 12, hour hand exactly on a number), then half past (minute hand on 6, hour hand between)
Teach that half past is 'the last number the hour hand has passed', not the number it is nearest

Link 'half past' to halves from fractions: the minute hand has travelled half way round

learn.summary: Children aged 5–6 read and draw o'clock and half-past times on an analogue clock. The crux is that the two hands measure different things and move together: at half past, the minute hand points to the 6 and the hour hand sits HALFWAY between two numbers. The time is read as 'half past the last number the hour hand has passed' — not the number it is nearest. Establish o'clock first, then half past, pairing reading with drawing in both directions.

activities.title: Wind the clock and watch the hour hand slide
feedback: If the hour hand looks like it should be on a number at half past, wind the clock slowly and watch: the hour hand never jumps — it is only halfway between the numbers when the minute hand is on the 6.
If you say 'half past 8' when the hour hand is between 7 and 8, trace back to the number the hour hand LEFT: it has passed the 7 but not yet reached the 8, so it is half past 7.
A geared or linked clock where moving one hand moves the other makes the proportional link visible; a clock whose hands move independently will not show this and can reinforce the error.
activities.rationale: The hour-hand-halfway position is the representational heart of half past and the most common error point. Watching the hands move together is intended to address the misconception that the hour hand points straight at a number at half past; the approach is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'

In interviews with Grades 2 and 4, the hour hand was significantly more challenging to position accurately than the minute hand, and a common approach was 'Number Matching' — matching a digit to a numeral on the clock — which was accurate only about half the time; students also treated hour and minute units separately (e.g. reading 7:00 as 'six o'clock').
learnerActions: On a geared teaching clock (one where turning the minute hand drives the hour hand in proportion), start at 7 o'clock with the minute hand on 12 and the hour hand exactly on the 7.
Slowly turn the minute hand clockwise (the way clock hands normally go: 12, 1, 2, 3…) round the face to the 6, and watch the hour hand crawl away from the 7 toward the 8.
Stop when the minute hand reaches the 6 — half a turn round — and check where the hour hand is: it sits exactly halfway between 7 and 8.
Say the time aloud as 'half past 7', naming which hand told you it was a HALF (the minute hand, half way round) and which told you the hour (the hour hand, past the 7).
Repeat starting from several other o'clock positions (3, 9, 11) so you see the same halfway pattern each time.
activities.intendedInsight: At half past, the hour hand is dragged halfway between two numbers by the minute hand's half turn; 'half past 7' means 'half way past 7', not 'hour hand on 7 or 8'.

activities.title: Name each hand before you read
feedback: If you read half past 3 as roughly '6 o'clock', you are reading the long (minute) hand as if it gave the hour — check the short hand for the hour instead.
Colour-coding and naming each hand's job first is intended to help guard against swapping their meanings.
Matching a hand to the nearest numeral ('number matching') is unreliable: in the cited interviews it gave the right answer only about half the time.
activities.rationale: Aims to target the hand-confusion and bare-number-matching errors by prompting interpretation of each hand's measured quantity before any reading; this is a proposal informed by the documented error patterns, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: In interviews with Grades 2 and 4, the hour hand was significantly more challenging to position accurately than the minute hand, and a common approach was 'Number Matching' — matching a digit to a numeral on the clock — which was accurate only about half the time; students also treated hour and minute units separately (e.g. reading 7:00 as 'six o'clock').
learnerActions: Look at a clock where the short hand (hour) and long hand (minute) are colour-coded differently.
Before saying any time, point to each hand and say its job: 'short hand = the hour', 'long hand = the minutes'.
Read several clocks (e.g. 3 o'clock, half past 9) always naming the hand first, then the time.
Deliberately spot a swapped reading: if someone treated the long (minute) hand as if it gave the hour, explain why that reading would be wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The two hands measure different quantities; reading a clock means interpreting what each hand tells you, not matching a hand to the nearest numeral.

activities.title: Draw the hands to show a time
feedback: If you draw the hour hand straight at the 7 for half past 7, compare with the geared clock: at half past the hour hand is always midway to the next number.
If you draw a long hour hand or short minute hand, recall that the short hand always shows the hour.
For 'half past 11', the hour hand goes halfway between 11 and 12, not on the 11 — this is the exact case where learners often go wrong.
activities.rationale: Drawing is a production task that requires constructing both hands. Unlike selecting among ready-made clocks (a recognition task), it can reveal whether a child places the hour hand between numbers — recognition alone does not elicit production. The curriculum explicitly requires drawing the hands.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'tell the time to the hour and half past the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times' (statutory), with non-statutory guidance to tell the time throughout the day 'first using o'clock and then half past'.

White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'
learnerActions: On a blank clock face, draw both hands for a given o'clock time (e.g. 3 o'clock): long minute hand on 12, short hour hand exactly on the 3.
On a fresh blank face, draw half past 7: minute hand on 6, and the hour hand drawn HALFWAY between the 7 and the 8.
Check your own drawing by asking: has the hour hand passed the 7 but not reached the 8? Is the minute hand on the 6?
Explain in words why the hour hand is between the numbers and not on one.
Try several more (half past 9, half past 11) and each time place the hour hand between the two numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Showing a time requires constructing both hands correctly — especially placing the hour hand between numbers for half past — which asks more of the child than recognising a correct clock.

activities.title: Which hour has it passed? (reasoning the half-past hour)
feedback: If you pick the number ahead (saying half past 4 when the hand is between 3 and 4), check which number the hand has gone past — it left the 3, so it is half past 3.
Connecting the minute hand's half turn to the idea of 'half' reinforces why the time is 'half past' rather than a whole hour.
The claim that the hour hand points to 11 at half past 11 is a classic error: it actually sits halfway between 11 and 12.
activities.rationale: Aims to address the 'nearest number' error and the number-matching habit by asking the learner to reason explicitly about which hour the hand has passed; a proposal informed by the documented misconception, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'
learnerActions: Look at a clock with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand between two numbers (e.g. between 3 and 4).
Decide whether it is half past 3 or half past 4, and state the rule you used.
Trace which number the hour hand has already LEFT and which it is heading toward.
Respond to the claim 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11' — explain why that is wrong and where the hour hand really goes.
Link to halves: the minute hand has travelled half way round the face, which is why we say 'half' past.
activities.intendedInsight: At half past you name the hour by the last number the hour hand has passed, not the number it is nearest or heading toward.

constraints: Use a geared or linked clock so the hour hand moves in proportion as the minute hand turns; a clock whose hands can be set independently will not show the proportional relationship and may reinforce the hour-hand-on-a-number error.
Establish o'clock (minute hand on 12, hour hand exactly on a number) before introducing half past (minute hand on 6, hour hand between numbers).
Always pair reading with drawing: given a time, draw both hands; given a clock, say the time.

Matching clocks to times by selecting among ready-made options is recognition, not construction; it does not reveal whether a child can place the hour hand correctly between numbers and should be followed by actual drawing.

A static labelled clock (e.g. tap-to-reveal names of the hands) can introduce which hand is which, but cannot show the two hands moving together or catch a mis-drawn hour hand; treat it as an introductory scaffold, not the main activity.
Colour-code the hands (short = hour, long = minute) and name each hand's job to help prevent swapping their meanings.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support general teaching principles (curriculum requirement, half-past structure, documented error patterns) but do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity proposed here; efficacy wording is kept qualified (intended/aims to).

Activity 1's winding step was corrected: a half turn of the minute hand (to the 6) places the hour hand halfway between the numbers; the earlier 'full turn' wording conflicted with stopping at the 6 and was adjusted for coherence.

The original research rated a planar/3D comparison and an in-role dialogue as poor fits; these catalog fit rankings were dropped as product-ranking boilerplate. A clock face is a 2D representation, but this does not establish a universal claim that no spoken or three-dimensional treatment could ever contribute.

No conceptual errors were found in the source's time content; the half-past structure (minute hand on 6, hour hand halfway, named by the last hour passed) is consistent with the cited curriculum and scheme of learning.

topic.description: Know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows there are 60 minutes in an hour, can they tell you how many minutes are in 2 hours — and how many hours make a whole day?

pedagogy.summary: Children learn the key time-unit facts — 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day — and use them in simple problems. Recall of the facts is usually secure; the conceptual work is grasping the non-decimal 60-grouping (time is NOT base-10) and that a whole day is two 12-hour sweeps of the clock (24, not 12). Taught by counting minutes in 60s on a clock/number line and tracking the hour hand's double sweep across day and night.
bestPractices: Count minutes in fives around the clock so 60 minutes visibly closes into one hour (the 60-grouping)
Track the hour hand round the clock twice — morning then night — to build 12 + 12 = 24, linking to am/pm and the 24-hour clock
Contrast time with money/base-10 explicitly: 60 minutes make an hour, not 100
Use simple duration problems (a 90-minute film) so children APPLY the facts, not just recite them
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock face
A number line marked in minutes and hours
A day-strip showing two 12-hour halves (day and night)
A 24-hour clock shown alongside the 12-hour clock
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12'
Over-applies base-10 — treats 1 hour as 100 minutes, 90 minutes as 9 hours, or half an hour as 50 minutes
Fails to regroup at 60 when adding times (3:40 + 30 minutes = 3:70)
Muddles which unit is larger (minute vs hour)

learn.summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) learn the key time-unit facts — 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day — and apply them in simple duration problems. Recall of the facts is usually secure; the real conceptual work is grasping the non-decimal 60-grouping (time is not base-10) and that a whole day is two 12-hour sweeps of the clock (24, not 12). The core approach is to count minutes in fives so a full 60 closes into one hour, and to track the hour hand's double sweep across day and night.

activities.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours
feedback: If a learner says a day is 12 hours because 'the clock stops at 12', have them watch/track the second lap explicitly, naming the pm hours on the first lap (midday to midnight) and then the am hours on the second lap (midnight to midday), so they see the 12 numbers reused.
If they reach 24 but can't explain it, ask them to point to where the first 12 hours end and the second 12 begin on the day-strip.
Reinforce by matching times across the 12-hour and 24-hour clocks (1pm = 13:00) so the double sweep is anchored to a familiar format.
activities.rationale: The 12-hour vs 24-hour structure is a documented conceptual challenge, not a recall gap; children must grasp that the clock counts midnight-to-midday and again midday-to-midnight (one lap = 12 hours, two laps = 24 hours). Watching the hour hand complete a second lap is intended to make the reuse of the 12 numbers concrete. A live day-strip that fills as the hand moves, and a side-by-side 24-hour clock, are optional ways to make the double sweep visible; a labelled static clock with tap-to-reveal, or a character/dialogue that states and quizzes the facts, can serve as lighter-weight alternatives, but neither lets the learner watch the sweep unfold.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).

The 12-hour vs 24-hour structure is a genuine conceptual challenge: in a Years 3-4 interview study, an item asking how long the hour hand takes to go once round scored 12 h as fully correct and 24 h as the partial/incorrect response, and the authors stress children must grasp that a 12-hour clock counts from midnight to midday and again from midday to midnight; meanwhile basic unit facts (seconds/minute, minutes/hour, months) were largely a strength (>90%), with the difficulties lying in the deeper relational/duration concepts.
learnerActions: Move the hour hand slowly round an analogue clock from midday, naming the hours aloud as it passes the numbers.
When the hand returns to 12, pause and count: that first lap covered 12 hours (midday through to midnight).
Send the hand round a second time, now naming the night and morning hours, and track a day-strip that fills behind the clock — one half for the first lap, the second half for the second lap.
Write down the total: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in a whole day and night.
Line a 12-hour clock up beside a 24-hour clock so that, for example, 1pm matches 13:00, confirming the numbers 1-12 get used twice.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole day is 24 hours because the hour hand goes round the 12-number clock face twice — once from midday to midnight and once from midnight to midday — so 12 + 12 = 24, not 12. One lap alone is 12 hours; it takes two laps to make a day.

activities.title: Closing the hour at 60: the non-decimal grouping
feedback: If a learner says 90 minutes is 9 hours (or 0.9 of an hour), count minutes in fives to 60 on the number line so a full 60 closes into one hour before applying it to 90.
If they add times like 3:40 + 30 = 3:70, show that past 60 the minutes roll over into the next hour (3:40 + 30 = 4:10).
If they say half an hour is 50 minutes, count in fives to the halfway point and confirm it is 30, because half of 60 is 30, not half of 100.
Praise correct regrouping by asking them to explain WHY it is 60 and not 100.
activities.rationale: Children apply discrete whole-number / base-10 reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the hour-minute relationship — not fact recall — is the crux. Counting minutes in fives is intended to make the 60-grouping concrete before it is applied to durations. An optional container that only closes at exactly 60 and overflows at 90 is intended to make the regrouping visible; a slider or fill-in item can then check that the learner regroups rather than reciting the bare fact.
sourceClaims: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard groupings of 12 and 60 (Kamii & Russell's 'inability to coordinate hierarchical units'), so the multiplicative hour-minute relationship, not fact recall, is the crux of difficulty.
Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Count minutes in fives around a clock face or along a number line marked in minutes, saying 5, 10, 15 … up to 60.
Notice that it takes exactly 60 minutes for the minute hand to complete one full lap (twelve jumps of 5), so 60 minutes close into 1 hour.
Contrast this with money/base-10 out loud: an hour is 60 minutes, NOT 100 — time does not group in tens and hundreds.
Fill an 'hour container' that only closes at 60: pour in 90 minutes and watch it overflow into one full hour (60) with 30 left over.
Record the result: 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes, because 90 = 60 + 30.
activities.intendedInsight: Minutes regroup into hours at 60, not at 100: a full 60 minutes makes one hour, so 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes — the grouping is felt by counting and overflowing, not just recited.

activities.title: Apply the facts: simple duration problems
feedback: Correct answer, no reason: ask them to show where the 60 or the double sweep is doing the work.
For the day item, a 12-hour answer signals the double-sweep misconception — return to tracking the hour hand round twice.
For the 90-minute item, a 9-hour or 0.9 answer signals missing 60-regrouping — return to counting minutes in fives to 60.
Mark as secure only when the learner states the fact AND explains it AND applies it to a new duration.
activities.rationale: Simple duration problems require learners to apply the facts rather than recite them; a learner can correctly state '60 minutes in an hour' yet still not USE the 60-grouping, and asking for the reason separates memorisation from understanding. Fact-recall and duration items (fill-in, multiple choice offering a 12-hour wrong option, a '90 minutes = [ ] hour [ ] minutes' item) are a valid quick check of application but should be paired with a 'why' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Solve a duration problem such as: 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?' and state the answer as 1 hour 30 minutes.
Answer a day question with reasoning: 'How many hours are in one whole day and night, and why — when the clock only shows 1 to 12?'
Decide which unit is larger, a minute or an hour, and justify it.
Explain each answer in words, not just give the number, so the reasoning is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: The time-unit facts are tools to be used: a learner who understands them can convert 90 minutes to 1 hour 30 and explain 24 hours as two 12-hour sweeps, transferring the reasoning to fresh problems.

constraints: Target the fact and its use, not the astronomy: the Earth-rotation cause of a 24-hour day is a different topic and is not the learning objective here.
Keep one-lap=12 hours and two-laps=24 hours distinct in all learner-facing wording; never state or imply that the hour hand goes 'once round' in 24 hours.

Recognition-only checks (multiple choice, fill-in) confirm recall and can catch some regrouping errors, but they do not by themselves show the learner can explain the double sweep or regroup a fresh duration — pair them with a 'why' prompt that elicits the reasoning.

A static labelled clock or day-strip, or a character/dialogue, can state the facts but does not let the learner watch the double sweep or the 60-grouping happen; treat these as lighter scaffolds, not replacements for counting/tracking the motion.
Explicitly contrast time with base-10 (60 not 100) rather than assuming learners will transfer money reasoning correctly; the base-10 over-application is the main error to pre-empt.
Half an hour is 30 minutes because half of 60 is 30; do not let '50 minutes' (half of 100) stand as an acceptable answer.

The cited Years 3-4 interview study reports that 24h was scored as the partial/incorrect response to 'how long the hour hand takes to go once round' — because one lap of the hour hand is in fact 12 hours, while a whole day (two laps) is 24 hours. The activities here keep this distinction explicit (one lap = 12h, two laps = 24h); reviewers should confirm learner-facing wording never conflates 'once round = 24h'.

probeDeeper: 'It is 12 o'clock in the middle of the day. When the hour hand gets back to 12 again, what time is it — and how many hours have gone by?'
'My clock says 2 o'clock. Could that be the middle of the night as well as the afternoon? How would we tell them apart?'
'Half an hour is how many minutes — and why isn't it 50?'
assess.correctAnswer: (A) 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice — 12 hours through the morning and 12 more through the afternoon and night, so 12 + 12 = 24. (B) 1 hour 30 minutes, because 60 minutes make one hour and 90 = 60 + 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a whole day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12' — doesn't realise the hour hand goes round twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it directly: track the hour hand through a full day, naming am then pm as two 12-hour sweeps, and line the 12-hour clock up against a 24-hour clock so 13:00 = 1pm.

The clock face only shows the numbers 1 to 12 — so how can a day have that many hours? Tell me why.' (B) 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?'
