pedagogy.summary: Children compare how long events last and put several in order by duration, and sequence intervals on a timeline. Because at this age they can't yet calculate elapsed time, comparison rests on measured or timed evidence (stopwatch, sand-timers) and on a common start. The deep hurdle carried from earlier is judging duration by non-time cues — a faster or further event, or the one that FINISHED later, is wrongly thought to have taken longer.
bestPractices: Compare timed events with a stopwatch / sand-timers so duration is measured, not guessed
Use a common start so 'who finished first' fairly shows quicker (a shorter duration)
Explicitly separate 'finished later' from 'took longer' with same-start and different-start cases
Order three durations by lining up their measured lengths (bars / timers)
Sequence intervals on a timeline of the day
keyRepresentations: Stopwatch / sand-timers giving a measured duration
Duration bars laid side by side for ordering
A common start-line for fair comparison
A daily timeline for sequencing intervals

Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring the start
Orders by how exciting or memorable an event was rather than its measured length
Treats a bigger clock-number at the end as a longer duration

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 6–7) compare how long events last, order several events by duration, and sequence intervals on a daily timeline. Because they are not yet expected to calculate elapsed time, comparison should rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatches, sand-timers, duration bars). A common start is needed specifically when using finishing order as the evidence of who was quicker; when starts differ, children compare the measured running length of each event instead. The central hurdle is judging duration by non-time cues: thinking the faster, further, more exciting, or later-finishing event 'took longer', or reading a later finishing clock time as a longer duration. (A stopwatch or timer started from zero at the start of each event is different: its end reading is the duration, so a bigger reading there does mean longer.) The strongest teaching separates measured duration from speed, distance, and finishing position.

activities.title: Timed race from a shared start line, then order the duration bars
feedback: If a learner orders by excitement or memorability, re-line-up the measured durations side by side and read the order off the lengths: 'Was the race longest because it FELT long, or because the timer showed the most? Let's check the timers.'
If a learner picks the faster or further event as longest, point back to the shared start: 'We both started together, so whoever stopped first took less time.'
Confirm correct ordering by having the learner trace each bar length and name the order shortest-to-longest.
activities.rationale: Making duration visible as a growing bar from a common start decouples 'how long' from speed and finishing excitement, directly targeting the time-speed-distance confusion. A live, draggable bar lets the child measure and order rather than guess. Comparing and sequencing intervals of time is an explicit Year 2 measurement expectation.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'compare and sequence intervals of time'.
Young children characteristically confuse duration with speed and distance (time-speed-distance confusion), judging that a faster or further-travelling object took more time.

Duration is the weakest area of children's time understanding in Years 3-4 (only about half reaching full understanding), so comparing and ordering durations warrants explicit measured-evidence teaching rather than being assumed.
learnerActions: Run or watch two or three timed events that all begin at the same common start (for example three sand-timers started together, or three classroom activities timed with a stopwatch).
Watch each event's duration grow as a bar (or sand-timer level) and note the moment it stops.
Arrange the finished bars/timers into order from shortest to longest duration — the order is simply the bar lengths.
Explain how you decided, pointing to the measured length rather than how fast or exciting each looked.
activities.intendedInsight: How long an event lasts is read from its measured duration, not from how fast, far, or exciting it was. With a common start, whoever stopped first took the shortest time.

activities.title: Different-start challenge: 'finished last' is not 'took longest'
feedback: If a learner picks whoever stopped last: 'This timer started late but stopped last — did it actually RUN for the most time? How can we tell?'

If a learner points to the later clock time showing when an event stopped and calls it longest, distinguish the two: a later clock time tells you WHEN it ended, not HOW LONG it ran — compare the measured running lengths from each start instead (a timer started from zero at each event's start would show that running length directly).
Reinforce by contrasting with the shared-start case: with a common start, finishing order does show duration; with different starts it does not.
Confirm reasoning when the learner measures each event's running length independently of its stop moment.
activities.rationale: The finished-later-equals-longer error specifically undermines simple duration comparison; deliberately staging a different-start case where the last-to-finish event is shortest confronts that error with measured evidence. Because the last-to-finish event also shows the later finishing clock time, this case likewise addresses reading a later end time as a longer duration (if each event were timed from zero, the shortest event would show the smaller reading). This is the discriminating case between salience/finish-position reasoning and genuine elapsed-time reasoning.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 8) documents that 'children may think that an event that ends at a later time must have a longer duration' — the finished-later-equals-longer misconception that also undermines simple duration comparison.
learnerActions: Watch a case where one event starts late but stops last, while its measured duration (bar/timer) is actually the shortest.
Decide which event ran for the most time, and justify using the actual running time rather than who stopped last or whose finishing clock time is later.
Compare a same-start case and a different-start case side by side, and say why the start time changes what finishing order tells you.
activities.intendedInsight: Stopping last only means 'took longest' when everything started together. When starts differ, you must compare how long each event actually ran, not who finished last or whose finishing clock time is later.

activities.title: Compare and sequence from timer readings
feedback: For a 'which took longer?' comparison, if the learner chooses the faster/further event, re-present two events that start together and ask which one is still going after the other stops, so duration is judged by running time rather than speed or distance.
Include a speed/distance counterexample in discussion: 'Both cars started together. The red car went further but the green one was still going after red stopped — which ran for more time?'
Confirm correct answers by having the learner name the measured value they used to decide.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering items from timer readings give clear, discriminating practice and check whether the child reasons from measured length. These are recognition/selection tasks, so they verify a decision but do not by themselves require the child to run and measure an event; pair them with the hands-on timing activities above.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'compare and sequence intervals of time'.
learnerActions: Look at two timers and decide which event took longer, explaining how the reading shows it.
Sequence three events by how long they took, using their timer readings or measured lengths.
Match each activity to its measured duration.
Place everyday intervals in order on a timeline of the day to sequence intervals of time.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing and ordering durations can be read directly from measured values, and intervals of a day can be sequenced in order.

constraints: Learners this age cannot yet calculate elapsed time, so comparison must rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatch, sand-timers, duration bars); a common start is required only when fair finishing-order reasoning is used to judge who was quicker.

Ordering by how exciting or memorable an event felt is common at this age and often improves with repeated measured evidence; respond by re-lining-up the measured durations side by side and reading the order off the lengths.

A static two-timer picture with tap-to-reveal can label longer/shorter but does not let the child measure and order events live; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for timing and arranging real durations.
Spoken commentary can invite comparison but does not itself supply the measured evidence that settles which event took longer; pair any discussion with timers or measured lengths.
Timer-reading comparison and matching are recognition tasks: they verify a decision but do not require the learner to independently run and measure events, so include hands-on timing too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed 3D adds nothing because comparing/ordering durations 'is not a spatial task'; this is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted. A 3D format is simply not needed here for the measured-comparison objective.

The original implied the 2D interactive is uniquely able to break the judge-by-speed/finish-position confusion. Measured timing and duration bars support this well, but comparative necessity over other measured-evidence approaches (e.g. real sand-timers) is not established by the cited sources; phrasing has been softened.

The Piaget time-speed-distance claim is marked verified:false in the source row; it is retained in sourceClaims as a well-known developmental observation but should not be treated as freshly verified.

The original's fourth misconception (a bigger end clock-number read as a longer duration) was not explicitly handled in the earlier candidate's learner text; it has been added to the different-start activity's actions and feedback, since the last-to-finish event also shows the larger stop reading.

The summary previously framed a common start as a general requirement for duration comparison; this was corrected to scope it to finishing-order reasoning, matching the different-start activity where events are compared by measured running length without a shared start.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare same-start, same-route events with a visible timer so duration is separated from speed; narrate 'we both started together, so whoever stopped first took less time'.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat this as a misconception to correct — ordering by salience rather than duration self-corrects with exposure. Instead, re-line-up the measured durations (bars or timers) side by side and read the order off the lengths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the three-event ordering puts the exciting event as 'longest' regardless of its timer

responseLevels.gap: Orders and compares by speed, distance, finishing position or excitement, not by measured duration.
responseLevels.full: Orders three durations and compares two by measured elapsed time, separating duration from speed, distance and finishing position, and transferring to a new comparison.

topic.name: Telling time to 5 minutes
topic.description: Tell and write the time to five minutes on analogue clocks, including quarter past and quarter to the hour, write these times in digital form, and draw clock hands to show them
evidence: Read an analogue clock showing 3:25 and write the time in digital form as 3:25
Write 'quarter past 9' as 9:15 and 'twenty to four' as 3:40
Draw clock hands to show twenty to four, with the minute hand on 8 and the hour hand just before 4
topic.assessmentPrompt: If the clock shows quarter to four, can {{name}} tell you the time — and draw hands on a blank clock face to show twenty past three?

pedagogy.summary: Children read and write time to five minutes — including quarter past and quarter to — and draw the hands. Two representational hurdles: reading the minute hand in fives (the minute hand on the 5 means 25 past, not 5), and the 'to' side, where times after half past belong to the NEXT hour and the hour hand sits over halfway toward it. 'Quarter to' is new and easily confused with 'quarter past'. Taught by counting round the clock in fives and using a past/to (right/left) split.
bestPractices: Count the minute intervals in fives round the clock so each number stands for a multiple of 5
Split the clock: right-hand side = 'past', left-hand side = 'to'
Teach that after half past, times are 'minutes to' the NEXT hour and the hour hand is over halfway between the two numbers
Contrast quarter past (hour hand just past a number) with quarter to (hour hand nearly at the next number)
Read AND write — analogue ↔ words ↔ digital (quarter past 9 / 9:15) — and draw the hands
keyRepresentations: A clock with the 5-minute counts marked around it
A past/to split clock (right = past, left = to)
A geared clock for the hour-hand position
Triple cards: words / analogue / digital (quarter past 9 – 9:15)
commonMisconceptions: Reads the minute-hand number directly (minute hand on 5 → '5 past' not 25 past; on 2 → '2 past' not 10 past)
Confuses quarter past and quarter to
After half past, keeps counting 'past' (35 minutes past) instead of switching to 'to' (25 to)
Names the wrong hour for a 'to' time, or puts the hour hand on a number instead of partway toward the next

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 read and write time to five minutes — including quarter past and quarter to — and draw the clock hands. Two representational hurdles dominate: reading the minute hand in fives (the minute hand on the 5 means 25 past, not 5), and the 'to' side, where times after half past are named in relation to the NEXT hour (although the digital hour stays as the earlier hour, e.g. quarter to 4 = 3:45) and the hour hand sits over halfway toward it. 'Quarter to' is new and easily confused with 'quarter past'. The core teaching moves are counting round the clock in fives and splitting the clock into a 'past' (right) and 'to' (left) side.

activities.title: Count round the clock in fives
feedback: If a learner reads 3:25 as 'five past three', pause and recount the fives aloud from the 12 to the 5 (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) and ask them to land on the number the hand actually reaches.
Confirm: minute hand on the 5, counted in fives, is 25; the hour hand sitting between the 3 and the 4 (not yet halfway) tells us the hour is still 3, so it is twenty-five past three.
For a minute hand on the 2, recount: 5, 10 — that is ten past, not two past.
activities.rationale: Counting the intervals in fives directly targets the most common error — reading the minute-hand numeral as the minutes — by making each number stand for its five-count before any real time is read.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.

The hour hand is significantly harder to position than the minute hand, and children frequently use 'Number Matching' (matching a digit to a clock numeral, accurate only ~half the time) and treat hour and minute units separately — the mechanism behind reading the minute-hand numeral directly and mis-placing the hour hand.
learnerActions: Starting at the 12, count the minute marks in fives round the clock, saying the running total at each number: 1→5, 2→10, 3→15, 4→20, 5→25, and so on.
Label (or tap, if using an interactive clock where each number lights its running five-count) each number with its minute value.
Then read a real clock showing 3:25: minute hand on the 5, hour hand between the 3 and the 4 but not yet halfway, so the hour is still 3. State the minutes as twenty-five, not five.
Repeat with other 'past' times to five minutes.
activities.intendedInsight: The number the minute hand points to is NOT the number of minutes — each number stands for its multiple of five, so the minute hand on the 5 means 25 minutes, not 5.

activities.title: The 'past' to 'to' switch at the bottom of the clock
feedback: If a learner gives a '35 past three' style answer for a left-side time, remind them they have crossed the bottom of the clock onto the 'to' side, and count the minutes back to the next hour (to four).
Check the named hour: on the 'to' side, we name the hour the hands are heading toward, not the one just left behind.

If an interactive clock is available, moving the minute hand across the 6 and watching 'twenty-five past' flip to 'twenty-five to' — with the named hour advancing — makes the switch visible; otherwise trace it with a finger on a geared clock.
activities.rationale: The right/past–left/to split and counting back from the 6 directly address the error of continuing to count 'past' after the half hour and naming the wrong hour.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.
learnerActions: Split the clock down the middle: the right-hand side is 'past', the left-hand side is 'to'.
Watch (or move the minute hand) as it travels from twenty-five past across the 6 and up the left side. As it crosses the bottom, start counting the minutes BACK to the next hour instead of forward.
Note that once past the half hour, the named hour becomes the NEXT hour, and the hour hand moves over halfway between the two numbers toward it.
Read twenty-five to four: minute hand on the 7, hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4 — and say why it is 'to four' and not '35 past three'.
activities.intendedInsight: After half past, we count the minutes remaining until the NEXT hour and name that next hour; the hour hand sits over halfway between the current and next number to show this.

activities.title: Quarter past versus quarter to, and placing the hour hand
feedback: If a learner draws twenty to four with the hour hand on the 3, point out the hour hand should be over halfway toward the 4 because it is nearly the next hour.
If quarter to 4 is read as quarter past 4, check which side of the clock the minute hand is on: the 9 is on the 'to' side, so it is quarter to.
Reinforce: quarter past = hour hand just past the number; quarter to = hour hand nearly at the next number.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting the two quarters and showing the hour hand's gradual position between numbers addresses the confusion of the two quarters and the habit of placing the hour hand on a number.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.

The hour hand is significantly harder to position than the minute hand, and children frequently use 'Number Matching' (matching a digit to a clock numeral, accurate only ~half the time) and treat hour and minute units separately — the mechanism behind reading the minute-hand numeral directly and mis-placing the hour hand.
learnerActions: Contrast two clocks: quarter past 9 (minute hand on the 3, hour hand just past the 9) and quarter to 4 (minute hand on the 9, hour hand nearly at the 4).
Say which side of the clock each is on (quarter past = right side; quarter to = left side) and which hour is named.

For a 'to' time, draw the hour hand over halfway toward the next number — NOT resting on a number. For quarter to 4, place the hour hand nearly at the 4; for twenty to four, place the hour hand over halfway from the 3 to the 4 with the minute hand on the 8.
Check: is the hour hand closer to the current number or the next number?
activities.intendedInsight: 'Quarter to' and 'quarter past' are different sides of the clock with different named hours; the hour hand moves gradually and, for 'to' times, sits part-way toward the next number rather than on a number.

activities.title: Translate between words, clock face, and digital
feedback: Check that drawn hands match: the minute hand lands on the correct number for the five-count and the hour hand is placed appropriately (on the 'to' side it should be part-way toward the next number).

When writing quarter past 9 as a digital time, confirm 15 minutes past, so 9:15; for quarter to, the minutes are 45 and the hour is still the earlier numeral (quarter to 4 = 3:45) — flag this as a point to watch when introducing digital 'to' times.

If an activity only asks learners to recognise or match a given answer, follow it with drawing or writing so the learner produces the time independently (recognition alone does not show they can produce it).
activities.rationale: Reading, writing, and drawing times on analogue clocks (production, not just recognition) is what the objective requires; linking these to the digital form is an extra connection that consolidates the representational links.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'tell and write the time to five minutes, including quarter past/to the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Match or build triple sets linking the same time across three forms: words ('quarter past 9'), an analogue clock face, and digital ('9:15').
Given a time in words, draw the hands on a blank clock to show it (e.g. draw twenty to four: minute hand on the 8, hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4).
Given an analogue clock, write the time in both words and digits.
Fill in the digital form of a worded time: 'quarter past 9 = 9:15'.
activities.intendedInsight: The same moment in time can be read, spoken, written in words, and written in digits, and the learner can move fluently between all of these forms including drawing the hands themselves.

activities.title: Rehearse saying times aloud
feedback: If a spoken time is wrong, return to the clock face and recount or re-split before saying it again.
Encourage full relative phrases ('quarter to four') rather than bare digits, since the wording is part of the objective.

Self-audit of time arithmetic (all consistent): quarter past = 15 minutes (9:15); quarter to 4 = 45 minutes past the hour = 3:45; twenty to four = minute hand on the 8 (5×8=40, i.e. 20 minutes to the next hour); twenty-five to four = minute hand on the 7 (35 minutes, i.e. 25 to); 3:25 = minute hand on 5. The original row's 3D rationale ('the clock face is planar; 3D adds nothing') was dropped as a catalog-ranking judgement rather than an objective pedagogical limit; it is not asserted here.

pedagogy.summary: Children extend telling time to reading the nearest FIVE minutes on an analogue clock, writing it in 12-hour digital notation, and labelling it a.m. or p.m. The procedure rests on counting the clock's 12 intervals in fives (each interval = 5 minutes, via the 5 times-table), deciding whether a time is 'past' (right of the 12-6 line) or 'to' (left) the hour, and — for digital — using a colon, not a decimal point. a.m./p.m. requires grasping that the same clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon and midnight.

Partition the clock vertically 12 to 6 to decide past (right) vs to (left) the hour
Match each analogue time to its 12-hour digital form and back, saying it aloud both ways
Anchor a.m./p.m. to real daily events (breakfast a.m., bedtime p.m.) and stress that each clock time happens twice a day
Record digital times with a colon, never a decimal point

learn.summary: Children extend telling time to reading analogue clocks to the nearest five minutes, writing that time in 12-hour digital notation (h:mm with a colon), labelling it a.m. or p.m., and rewriting it in 24-hour notation (hh:mm). The core procedure: count the clock's 12 intervals in fives so each numeral maps to its minute value (numeral 4 -> 20 minutes, not 4); use a vertical 12-to-6 partition to decide 'past' (right) versus 'to' (left) the hour, with 'to' times named against the NEXT hour; anchor a.m./p.m. to real daily events, understanding that each clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon and midnight; and convert to 24-hour time (from 1 p.m. onwards add 12 to the hour, so 3:40 p.m. = 15:40; a.m. hours stay the same, written with two digits, e.g. 8:05 a.m. = 08:05; the 12 o'clock hour after midnight becomes 00, e.g. 12:15 a.m. = 00:15, and the noon hour stays 12, e.g. 12:15 p.m. = 12:15). Activities below include a manipulable clock (preferred), practice/discrimination tasks, a static labelling scaffold, and an elicitation conversation, each with its own pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Drag the minute hand and watch the count-in-fives and digital readout
feedback: If the child reads the numeral literally (4 -> '4 minutes past'), re-run the count-in-fives tape aloud pairing each numeral with x5 until the 4 -> 20 link is fluent.
If the child keeps counting past the half hour ('40 past 3' for 3:40), point to the 12-6 partition: right is past, left is to, and 'to' times belong to the NEXT hour, so 3:40 is 'twenty to four'.

If the child treats the time as a decimal (e.g. thinks 3.50 means half past three, or that minutes run up to 99), model the colon convention and count the real 60 minutes on the dial to show the hour is 60, not 100.
If the child assigns a.m./p.m. by how late it feels, slide the day-strip marker so the same hand position lands once in the morning and once after noon, 12 hours apart.
activities.rationale: Reading to five minutes, the past/to decision, the analogue-to-digital rewrite and the twice-a-day idea are live-state relationships; letting the child move the hand and see the tape, readout, partition and day-strip respond is intended to make the numeral-to-minutes rule and the twice-a-day split visible rather than merely stated. The tape, 12-6 highlighter and day-strip marker are concrete feedback examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'tell and write the time from an analogue clock ... and 12-hour and 24-hour clocks' and 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute ... use vocabulary such as o'clock, am/pm, morning, afternoon, noon and midnight'.

White Rose Y3 Time documents the exact pupil errors: reading the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes ('minute hand on 4 -> 4 minutes past'); confusing times past and to; writing a decimal point instead of a colon; thinking there are 100 minutes in an hour (50 past 3 = 50 to 4); confusing am/pm ('1 am should be 1 pm because it is late'); and not knowing noon/midnight or that times occur twice a day. Models: count the 12 intervals in fives (5x table), vertical 12-6 partition for past/to.

Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to clock reading and struggle to coordinate the non-standard groupings of 12 and 60; the hour hand is significantly harder to read than the minute hand, and hour and minute are often read separately.
learnerActions: Drag the minute hand around a moveable-hands clock and watch a 'count in 5s' tape (5, 10, 15, 20...) unroll around the rim as a digital readout ticks alongside.
Pause when the minute hand reaches the numeral 4 and confirm the tape and readout say 20 minutes, not 4 — then do the same for numeral 8 (40 minutes).
Watch a vertical 12-to-6 line shade one colour on the right (past) and another on the left (to), and read 3:40 aloud as 'twenty TO four'.

Flip an a.m./p.m. toggle that slides a marker along a day-strip so the SAME hand position recurs 12 hours later — once in the morning (e.g. 8 o'clock breakfast, a.m.) and again 12 hours on in the evening (p.m.).
Write the shown time as h:mm using a colon with its a.m./p.m. label (e.g. 3:25 p.m.), then rewrite it in 24-hour notation (e.g. 15:25; 8:05 a.m. = 08:05).
activities.intendedInsight: Each clock numeral stands for its five-times value, 'to' times are named against the next hour, and every clock position recurs 12 hours later, so each clock time happens twice in one day, split at noon and midnight.

activities.title: Read, convert and sort: discrimination practice
feedback: '3:40' is 'twenty to four', not 'forty past three' — the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line, so name it against the next hour.
When a child treats the minutes as a decimal (e.g. 3.50 read as half past three), re-show the colon convention and count the 60 minutes on the dial so the hour is 60, not 100.
If a.m./p.m. sorting goes by 'how late it feels', revisit the noon/midnight split and that each clock time occurs twice a day.
activities.rationale: Matching, forced-choice and sorting items score cleanly and make natural discriminating items that help distinguish a child who runs the procedure from one who reads the numeral or display literally. Recognition and selection practice checks and rehearses the rule but does not by itself require the child to physically work the hands or construct the reading from scratch.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time documents the exact pupil errors: reading the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes ('minute hand on 4 -> 4 minutes past'); confusing times past and to; writing a decimal point instead of a colon; thinking there are 100 minutes in an hour (50 past 3 = 50 to 4); confusing am/pm ('1 am should be 1 pm because it is late'); and not knowing noon/midnight or that times occur twice a day. Models: count the 12 intervals in fives (5x table), vertical 12-6 partition for past/to.
learnerActions: Match analogue clock faces (with a.m./p.m. given) to their 12-hour and 24-hour digital times (and back), e.g. twenty to four in the afternoon = 3:40 p.m. = 15:40.
Answer discriminating questions such as 'Is 3:40 forty past three or twenty to four?'
Sort daily activities (breakfast, school, bedtime) into a.m. and p.m.
Write a shown clock as h:mm, using a colon.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure practice separates past from to, maps analogue to digital, and connects a.m./p.m. to everyday events, while surfacing residual errors.

activities.title: Label the fives on a fixed clock face (scaffold)
feedback: If a numeral is read as its face value, re-reveal and count the fives aloud from the 12.

Because the hands do not move, it cannot let the child convert a chosen time to digital or experience the twice-a-day split, so it serves as a scaffold toward the manipulable activity rather than a replacement for it.

activities.title: Talk about your day: eliciting a.m./p.m.
feedback: If a child says 1 a.m. 'should be' 1 p.m. because it feels late, place both on the day-timeline — 1 a.m. just after midnight and 1 p.m. just after noon — to show they are different moments.
If a child cannot place noon or midnight, mark them as the two split points on the timeline where a.m. and p.m. change over.
If a child thinks an unlabelled 3:40 is a single moment, show it occurs twice a day, once in the a.m. and once in the p.m.
activities.rationale: A short spoken exchange can prompt the child to use a.m./p.m. vocabulary in meaningful daily contexts and expose how they reason about morning/afternoon and about noon/midnight. Conversation elicits and consolidates the labelling but does not let an adult watch the hand-reading procedure, so pair it with the reading tasks.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'tell and write the time from an analogue clock ... and 12-hour and 24-hour clocks' and 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute ... use vocabulary such as o'clock, am/pm, morning, afternoon, noon and midnight'.
learnerActions: Answer questions like 'What time do you have breakfast? Is that a.m. or p.m.?' and 'What about when you go to bed?'
Place named daily events on a day-timeline split at noon and midnight.
Identify which 12 o'clock is noon and which is midnight, and say where on the timeline a.m. changes to p.m. and back.
Explain, for a given event, whether the clock time is in the morning or after noon.
Given a digital time with no label (e.g. 3:40), say how many different moments in one day it could be and why.

constraints: Secure recall of the 5 times-table underpins fluent counting of minutes; weak recall blocks fluent counting of the minutes, so rehearse it alongside clock reading. (It does not by itself block the past/to or a.m./p.m. reasoning.)

Write digital times with a colon (the convention used here; some styles write 3.25 with a full stop, but the separator is never a decimal point); the hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so '50 past 3' is 'ten to 4', not '50 to 4' via base-10 reasoning.
'To' times must be named against the NEXT hour (3:40 = 'twenty to four'), decided by whether the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line.
a.m./p.m. must be grounded in the noon/midnight split and the fact that each clock time occurs twice a day, not in how 'late' a time feels.

The static tap-to-reveal face and the conversation are scaffolds: the first cannot move hands or convert to digital; the second cannot show the reading method. Use them to support, not replace, work with moveable hands.
Recognition, matching and sorting tasks check and rehearse the rule but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading from scratch or physically set the hands.

This comparative/necessity claim is a catalog fit judgement not established by the cited sources, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as a pedagogical law; the original wording is flagged in the audit for reviewers.

The legacy fit rankings and product-format/quiz-step vocabulary and internal IDs were removed; the underlying pedagogical ideas (static labelling, dialogue elicitation) were retained as scaffold activities with stated limits.

Cited sources support the curriculum expectations and the catalogue of pupil errors and models; they do not establish comparative efficacy of the manipulable format over others. No efficacy claim is made here; efficacy wording is kept to 'intended/proposed'.

The reliable method is counting ON from the start to the end on a number line — jumping to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then whole hours, then the remaining minutes — NOT column subtraction, which fails when the hour is crossed because time is base-60, not base-10. Comparing two durations then follows from calculating each.

learn.summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times by counting ON from start to end on a number line: first bridge to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then add whole hours, then add the remaining minutes. Make explicit WHY column subtraction breaks when the end minutes are smaller than the start minutes, so you have to borrow across the hour (e.g. 4:10 − 2:50). Time is base-60 (60 minutes in an hour), not base-10. Comparing two durations follows from calculating each; a later end time does not by itself mean a longer duration.

activities.title: Build the jumps on a number line
feedback: General bridging slip (applies to any start time): if the learner makes the jump to the next o'clock too large — e.g. treating 10:15 → 11:00 as +85, or jumping 2:50 → 3:00 by more than +10 — remind them the minutes only run to 60. For 2:50 the jump to 3:00 is +10 (50 + 10 = 60); for 10:15 the jump to 11:00 is +45 (15 + 45 = 60).

If they skip the o'clock jump and land on the wrong minute, rebuild the three-part jump for the activity's own example: next o'clock first (2:50 → 3:00), then whole hours (3:00 → 4:00), then leftover minutes (4:00 → 4:10).

Column slip (a misconception, not a valid method): if, on the activity's 4:10 − 2:50 line-up or any hour-crossing subtraction, they 'borrow' as in base-10 (producing results like 0:85 for 11:00 − 10:15), show that base-10 borrowing assumes 100 minutes in an hour. An hour is 60 minutes, so counting on across the o'clock is the safe method.
activities.rationale: Seeing the jumps assemble the total, and seeing how column subtraction misleads at the minutes column, makes the base-60 structure visible as the child acts. Where a build-your-own number line is available, dragging each jump from the start time with an auto-shown bond to 60 and a running total, plus a 'try column subtraction' option that lines up end minus start, may make the mechanism concrete; a static annotated number line can show one worked example but cannot let the child build the jumps.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 8-9) documents that children may think an event ending at a later time must have a longer duration, and may attempt to calculate duration using column subtraction (end minus start), which leads to problems when hours are crossed; the recommended model is a number line with jumps and number bonds to the next hour.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, which explains column-subtraction errors and base-10 slips when crossing the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Start at the first time (e.g. 2:50) on a blank number line.
Make the first jump to the next o'clock (2:50 → 3:00, a +10 jump) and say the number bond to 60 that produced it (50 + 10 = 60).
Make whole-hour hops next (3:00 → 4:00, +1 hour).
Add the remaining minutes (4:00 → 4:10, +10).
Keep a running total of the jumps to assemble the duration (1 hour 20 minutes).

Compare this count-on method with column subtraction: line up 4:10 − 2:50 and notice the minutes column needs borrowing, and that borrowing as if there were 100 minutes in an hour goes wrong, because the minutes are base-60, not base-10.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting on from start to end — bridging the o'clock, adding whole hours, then the remaining minutes — gives the duration reliably, and column subtraction misleads across the hour unless you remember an hour holds 60 minutes, not 100.

activities.title: Calculate then compare two durations
feedback: If the learner picks the activity that ends later without calculating, have them count on for BOTH events first, then compare the two lengths.
Use a short activity that ends late against a long one that ends early (e.g. the 8:55–9:00 versus 8:00–8:50 pair) to decouple end-time from duration.
On the crossing-the-hour item (2:50 → 4:10), a base-10 or nonsense answer signals column subtraction — return to counting on and the o'clock bridge.
activities.rationale: Anchoring problems in real start/end times (lessons, films, TV programmes) and requiring both durations to be calculated before comparing targets the 'later end = longer' misconception directly. Crossing-the-hour and decoupled end-time items are natural discriminators. These can be posed as questions, fill-in-the-blank sums, or spoken word problems; a character can pose start/end problems but cannot observe the counting-on method, so pair posed problems with the learner showing their jumps.

learnerActions: Read a problem such as 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it?' and count on to find 45 minutes.
Work a crossing-the-hour problem: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' bridging to 3:00, adding 1 hour, then +10 to reach 1 hour 20 minutes.
Compare two events, e.g. an activity from 2:20 to 3:00 versus one from 6:15 to 6:50, by calculating each duration (40 minutes vs 35 minutes) and only then deciding which is longer.

pedagogy.summary: Children read and write time to the EXACT minute. The efficient procedure is NOT counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on the extra minutes (e.g. 23 past = 4x5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a further step: converting minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour (44 past 3 = 16 to 4, a number bond to 60). Reading the hour hand precisely also matters — near the top of the hour it sits almost on the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST PASSED.
bestPractices: Teach 'find the 5-minute interval before the hand, then count on' rather than counting every minute from 12
Use a number line / number bond to 60 to convert minutes past to minutes to
Check the hour hand carefully: at 7:43 the hour hand is nearly on 8 but the hour is still 7
Match analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
Rehearse the multi-step 'minutes to' reading, where errors cluster

Counting on from the last multiple of five
Number line for past-to-to conversion; part-whole bond to 60
Paired analogue and digital displays
commonMisconceptions: Counts individual minutes from 12 to the hand instead of counting on from the nearest 5 below (slow and error-prone)
Multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down (miscounts the bond to 60)
Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes '8:43' (hour hand almost on 8)
Reads a digital time literally rather than converting it (says 'seven forty-three' but can't render it on analogue or as a 'to' time)

learn.summary: Children read and write time to the exact minute on analogue and digital clocks. The efficient method is not counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on (e.g. 23 past = 4×5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a conversion step: turning minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour using a number bond to 60 (44 past 3 = 16 to 4). The hour hand also needs care: late in the hour it moves close to the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST passed (at 7:43 the hour hand is about three-quarters of the way to 8, but the hour is still 7; at 9:57 it is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9).

activities.title: Count on from the last five on a moveable clock
feedback: If the child counts every minute from the 12, prompt: 'Which five has the hand just passed?' then count on only the extra minutes from there.

If the child reads 7:43 as 8:43, say: 'The hour is the number the hour hand has LAST passed — it is still before the 8, so the hour is 7.' Slowly sweep the hour hand across the whole hour so they see it travel from just-past-7 to the 8.
For 9:57, if the child says 10, point out the hand has not yet reached the 10, so the hour is still 9 — read last-passed, not nearest.
Confirm a correct reading by restating the method: 'You found 40, then counted on 3 — that's 43, and the hour hand is still past 7, so 7:43.'
activities.rationale: Guidance documenting this error reports children count individual minutes to the hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and recommends the 4×5=20 then +3 method. A moveable clock lets the child rehearse the count-on procedure and watch the hour hand travel; a static annotated clock can still show one worked example but does not let the child try the count themselves.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.

The hour hand is significantly harder for children to read than the minute hand, and children tend to read hour and minute separately; near the top of the hour the hour hand's position (just before the next numeral) is a documented source of error.
learnerActions: On a clock with moveable hands and a minute scale (tick marks), set the minute hand to a target such as 43 minutes.
Find the last 5-minute mark the hand has passed (40) by counting the fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40.
Count on the extra single minutes from there: 41, 42, 43 — do not count all 43 ticks one at a time from the 12.
Check the hour hand: notice it has moved about three-quarters of the way toward the next numeral, and say the hour as the number it has LAST passed.
Try another near-the-hour example: set 9:57 — the hour hand is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9 because that is the number it has last passed.
Read the whole time aloud (e.g. 'forty-three minutes past seven' / 'seven forty-three').
activities.intendedInsight: The quick, reliable way to read exact minutes is to land on the nearest 5-minute mark below the hand and count on the remaining minutes, and to read the hour as the numeral the hour hand has last passed.

activities.title: Convert 'past' to 'minutes to' with a bond to 60
feedback: If the child gives a wrong 'to' time such as '23 to 8' for 7:43, bring back the number line: 'How many more from 43 to reach 60?' (17), so it is 17 to 8.
If the child cannot convert at all, rehearse just the bond to 60 first (e.g. 43 + ? = 60) before returning to the clock; do not re-teach whole-clock reading.
Watch that the stated hour is the NEXT hour (8, not 7) when giving a 'to' time.
activities.rationale: The multi-step 'minutes to' reading is where errors cluster, and a number line / part-whole bond to 60 is the recommended scaffold for the past-to-to conversion. Isolating the conversion step from the reading step targets the specific breakdown.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.
learnerActions: Start from an exact 'past' reading such as 43 minutes past 7.
On a number line from 0 to 60 (or a part-whole bond), find how far it is from 43 up to 60: 43 + 17 = 60.
State the 'to' time: 43 past 7 is 17 minutes to 8.
Repeat with other examples, e.g. 44 past 3 = 16 to 4; 57 past 9 = 3 to 10.
Say both forms of the same time aloud to connect them.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a 'to' time is one extra step on top of reading the 'past' time: use a number bond to 60 to find the gap to the next hour, and remember the hour named is the NEXT hour.

activities.title: Match and write analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
feedback: If a digital reading is copied literally but cannot be set on analogue (reads 'seven forty-three' but cannot place the hands or give the 'to' form), practise placing the minute hand at the counted-on position and sweeping the hour hand to just-past the hour.
For the hour-hand check: the answer is 7 because the hand has not yet reached 8 — read last-passed, not nearest.
For the fill-in: 44 + 16 = 60, so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4.
activities.rationale: Matching analogue to digital to the exact minute, the hour-hand question, and past-to conversion are the curriculum reading/writing/converting targets. Writing and hand-setting require the child to produce a time, not just recognise one; a recognition-only check would not show whether the child can construct the reading independently.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute'; Year 4 pupils 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks', so reading to the nearest minute is the age-8+ consolidation of this strand.
learnerActions: Read an analogue clock set to 7:43 and write it as a digital time.
Given a digital time such as 11:06, set the hands: minute hand just past the 1 (at the 6-minute tick), hour hand just past the 11.
Match several analogue faces to their digital equivalents to the exact minute.
For each, say the hour it has last passed and the minutes found by counting on.
Answer targeted checks, e.g. 'The hour hand is almost on 8 — what is the hour?' and 'Fill in: 44 minutes past 3 = ___ minutes to 4.'
activities.intendedInsight: Exact-minute times can be translated faithfully between analogue and digital in both directions, keeping the count-on method and the last-passed hour.

constraints: A static labelled clock can display one worked time but does not let the child rehearse the count-on procedure or watch the hour hand travel; use it as a worked example, not as the main practice.
Prompted oral readings (a character asking 'what time is it?') can elicit answers but do not reveal HOW the child finds the minutes; pair them with tasks where the method is visible.
Recognition/matching tasks assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading or set the hands; include writing and hand-setting for production.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: lighting the 5-minute marks in groups up to the last interval in one colour, then single count-on minutes in another colour; a toggle that rolls the reading round a 0–60 number line to show the 'to' form; an hour hand that creeps toward the next numeral so the child must read last-passed. These are illustrative, not required.
When scaffolding a child who counts single minutes, do not reteach clock reading from scratch — prompt them to the nearest five and count on.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 4×5=20 then +3 = 23 (correct); 43+17=60 so 7:43 is 17 to 8 (correct); 44+16=60 so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4 (correct); 57+3=60 so 57 past 9 = 3 to 10 (correct); for 11:06 the minute hand sits at the 6-minute tick just past the 1 (correct); for 9:57 the hour hand is nearly on 10 but the hour is still 9 (correct).
The '23 to 8' value is a documented learner ERROR, not a correct answer, and is used only as a feedback example to correct — never offered as a valid option.

The hour-hand rule ('the hour is the number the hour hand has last passed') is the key conceptual correction and is taught directly in activity 1 so the 'nearest numeral' error is fixed, not merely flagged. Independent re-check confirms the 9:57 example is present in activity 1 actions and feedback.
The source's catalog claim that '3D adds nothing' has been omitted as a comparison not established as a pedagogical fact; nothing here depends on it.

Independent review found no critical learner-facing errors; the arithmetic, hour-hand logic, and both-direction conversions are coherent from first action through final feedback. Remaining uncertainty is confined to unre-verified source evidence.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn that there are 60 seconds in a minute, the names and lengths of the twelve months, and that a leap year has 366 days occurring every four years. The second/month facts are usually recalled well; the conceptual depth is the irregular month-length pattern, the non-decimal 60-grouping for seconds and minutes, and — hardest — WHY a leap year exists: the Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun, so a day is added every four years. Most children do not connect time units to the Earth's motion at all.
bestPractices: Anchor the months and their lengths on a real calendar with a mnemonic (knuckles, or '30 days hath September'), revisiting the irregular 31/30/28 pattern
Count seconds into minute-groups on a timer so the 60-grouping (not 100) is felt
Explain the leap year through the Earth's orbit — the extra ~quarter-day each year accumulating into one whole day every four years — rather than as an arbitrary rule
Use the four-year cycle concretely (which recent years were leap years? when is the next?)
keyRepresentations: A wall calendar / year-strip divided into 12 months
The knuckle mnemonic for month lengths
A stopwatch or number line marked in seconds
A four-year calendar cycle showing February gain a 29th day
An Earth-orbit model linking the year to one revolution

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds learning time-unit and calendar facts: 60 seconds in a minute, the names and irregular lengths of the twelve months, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years. Factual recall of seconds/minutes and month names is usually a strength; the conceptual depth lies in (1) the uneven 31/30/28 month-length pattern (February has 29 days in a leap year), (2) the non-decimal grouping of 60 for seconds and minutes, and (3) WHY leap years exist - the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun, so the leftover quarter-days add up to about one extra day every four years. (Because the true leftover is slightly less than a quarter, a few century years such as 1900 and 2100 are not leap years; this detail is beyond the core objective.) Research reports most children do not connect time units to the Earth's motion at all.

activities.title: Advance a four-year calendar cycle and watch February change
feedback: If a learner expects every February to have 29 days, replay the cycle slowly and have them count: three turns at 28, only the fourth at 29.
If a learner says all months are the same length, have them read off the popped lengths and group them into 31-day, 30-day, and 'other' (February) piles.
If a learner can state '366 every four years' but not why, pair this with the orbit activity so the extra day has a cause, not just a count.
activities.rationale: Showing the extra day appear only on the fourth cycle makes the four-year period concrete rather than a recited rule; revealing each month's length makes the irregular pattern visible. A live dial lets the learner advance year-by-year and watch February change - an optional interaction that makes the cycle observable. This is a proposed design, not a measured intervention.
learnerActions: Step through four years one at a time on a calendar dial or a strip showing four Februaries in a row.
On years one, two and three, note that February has 28 days; on the fourth year watch a 29th day appear and the year-counter go from 365 to 366.
Say aloud what changes and what stays the same across the four years, then predict which upcoming calendar year will be the next leap year.
Tap or reveal each month in turn to pop up its length, and sort or describe the uneven 31/30/28 pattern as a shape, not just a list.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Every four years' is not an arbitrary rule to memorise - the extra day actually appears only on the fourth turn, and February is the month that gains it, while month lengths follow a lumpy repeating pattern.

activities.title: Build the leap day from the Earth's orbit
feedback: If a learner says the extra day is added 'to make the number even' or 'just because', show the four quarter-days accumulating so the day has a physical source.
If a learner thinks the quarter-day disappears each year, point to the set-aside tokens: the leftover is saved, not lost, until four of them make a whole day.
activities.rationale: Research reports that about 78% of Years 3-4 students did not connect time with the Earth's revolution around the Sun, even though a calendar year is based on one revolution of the Earth around the Sun (while a day comes from one spin of the Earth); building the quarter-day accumulation is intended to address this documented gap. The stated topic is the fact and cycle rather than full orbital mechanics, so keep the model simple and focused on the leftover-day accumulation. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: In a Years 3-4 interview study, 78% of students did not connect the notion of time with the Earth rotating on its axis or revolving around the Sun — even though calendars measure days from one revolution — while basic facts such as the number of seconds in a minute and the months of the year were largely a strength (>90% correct).
learnerActions: Using an orbit model, card tokens, or a tally, give each year its length as 'about 365 and a quarter days' and set aside the leftover quarter each year.
After four years, snap the four leftover quarter-days together into one whole extra day.
Explain in your own words where the extra day came from and why we only add it roughly every four years, then name the day we add it to (29 February).
activities.intendedInsight: The leap day exists because the Earth's orbit takes about 365 and a quarter days; the leftover quarter-day each year builds up to one whole day about every four years, which we add to February.

activities.title: Group seconds into minutes at exactly 60
feedback: If a learner writes '1 minute 30 seconds = 130 seconds', have them count the first minute as 60 seconds on the timer, then add 30 to get 90.
If a learner says 90 seconds is 0.9 of a minute, show that a full minute closes only at 60, so 90 seconds is one minute (60) plus 30 more - i.e. one and a half minutes, not 0.9.
Reinforce that the minute 'closes' at 60 before any leftover seconds are counted into the next minute.
activities.rationale: Research reports children apply discrete whole-number and base-10 reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the difficulty lies in converting rather than recalling the fact. Counting seconds into minute-groups on a stopwatch or number line is intended to make the 60-grouping felt before it is applied to conversions. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so converting between seconds and minutes (rather than recalling the fact) is where difficulty lies.
learnerActions: Count seconds on a stopwatch or a number line marked in seconds, and mark where a full group of 60 closes into one minute.
Work out how many seconds are in one and a half minutes, saying why it is 90 (60 + 30) and not 150 - rather than applying base-10 place value (treating 1.5 minutes as 1.5 x 100 = 150 seconds).
Convert a two-way example such as '1 minute 30 seconds = [ ] seconds' and '90 seconds = [ ] minute [ ] seconds', regrouping at 60 each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Seconds and minutes group in 60s, not 100s, so conversions require regrouping at 60 rather than applying base-10 place value.

activities.title: Recall and sort the facts
feedback: If month lengths are muddled, anchor them on a real wall calendar and revisit the irregular 31/30/28 pattern with the mnemonic.
If a learner thinks February always has 28 days, connect back to the four-year cycle where it gains a 29th.
Fact recall alone does not show the learner understands why a leap year happens; follow correct recall with a 'why' question.
activities.rationale: Naming, sorting and stating facts consolidate the statutory recall content, which research reports children generally find to be a strength (>90% correct). A sort or fact item can check classification and recall but does not by itself elicit the explanation of cause or the regrouping skill, so it is a foundation, not the whole objective. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year and leap year' (statutory Measurement content).

In a Years 3-4 interview study, 78% of students did not connect the notion of time with the Earth rotating on its axis or revolving around the Sun — even though calendars measure days from one revolution — while basic facts such as the number of seconds in a minute and the months of the year were largely a strength (>90% correct).
learnerActions: Name the months in order and state how many days each has.
Sort the months into 31-day, 30-day, and 'other' (February) groups.
Answer fact questions: '1 minute = [ ] seconds', 'how often is a leap year?', 'how many days in a leap year?'
Use a mnemonic such as knuckles or '30 days hath September' to recall which months are shorter.
activities.intendedInsight: The core recall facts - 60 seconds, month names and lengths, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years - need to be fluent so attention can go to the harder conceptual links.

constraints: Fact-recall items (naming months, stating '60 seconds', multiple-choice on leap-year frequency) check recall and classification but do not by themselves elicit the causal explanation of leap years or the regrouping skill for seconds/minutes; always pair recall with a 'why' or a conversion task.

A static calendar or year-strip with tap-to-reveal month lengths can name the facts and show the irregular pattern, but cannot run the four-year cycle or demonstrate the 60-grouping dynamically; use it as a naming scaffold, not as the full objective.

A character explaining months and leap years can introduce the facts; the four-year cycle and the 60-grouping may be easier to follow through a worked or observed sequence, though the cited sources do not establish this comparison. Treat the character as an introduction scaffold.
Keep the orbit model focused on the quarter-day accumulation; the objective is the leap-year fact and cycle, not full orbital mechanics.
Mnemonics (knuckles, '30 days hath September') aid recall of month lengths but do not teach why leap years occur; treat them as memory aids only.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness is claimed.

The leap-year rule is an approximation: a year is about 365.2422 days and the full civil rule skips some century leap years (e.g. 1900 is not a leap year, 2000 is). The '365 and a quarter days, one extra day every four years' framing matches the source material and is age-appropriate for 7-8 year olds, but is a simplification; flagged for awareness, not corrected in the learner-facing activities.

Self-audit of conversions: 1 minute 30 seconds = 90 seconds (60 + 30); 2 and a half minutes = 150 seconds (60 + 60 + 30). The source assessment's probe answer '250' and distractors '130'/'0.9 of a minute' are intentional wrong-answer examples addressed as misconceptions, never taught as correct. In the seconds activity the '0.9' misconception is confined to the reverse-direction feedback (90 seconds read as 0.9 of a minute), and '150' is used only as a base-10 distractor for 'one and a half minutes', which is genuinely wrong for that quantity.

The original source labelled a 3D calendar as adding 'nothing' and a static image as unable to 'run' the cycle, and called telling inferior to showing; these are reframed as scaffold affordances/limits with hedged wording rather than universal claims about what any medium can or cannot teach.
