topic.assessmentPrompt: If a train timetable shows a departure at 14:35, can {{name}} convert that to 12-hour clock time — and tell you whether that's morning or afternoon?

pedagogy.summary: Children read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation, and represent them on analogue clocks. The core rules: for p.m. times 1:00-11:59, ADD 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 on, SUBTRACT 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (not 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The rule must be applied ONLY to the right times — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps.
bestPractices: Ground the +12/-12 rule in the day: a day is 24 hours starting at midnight 00:00, and the afternoon/evening hours continue counting on past 12
Pair the same time in 12-hour and 24-hour form and ask 'what is the same, what is different?'
Stress the four-digit format with a leading zero for single-digit hours (09:45)
Handle the boundary cases explicitly: midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00, and 12:01-12:59 p.m. stay as 12:xx
Decide first whether the time is before or after noon — only p.m. times get +12
keyRepresentations: Paired 12-hour and 24-hour digital displays
Analogue clock for representing a converted time
A 12-hour to 24-hour conversion table
The 24-hour day-line (00:00 midnight -> 12:00 noon -> back to 00:00)
commonMisconceptions: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
Adds 12 to a.m. times too (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38')
Writes midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00
When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m. on the answer

learn.summary: Learners read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation and show them on analogue clocks. Core rules: for p.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59, add 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 onward, subtract 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (never 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The decisive step is deciding FIRST whether a time is before or after noon — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps where learners wrongly apply the rule.

activities.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
feedback: If a learner reads a morning time and adds 12, point to the day-line: the marker is before noon, so for the morning hours 1 a.m. to 11 a.m. the 24-hour and 12-hour hour numbers match (apart from the leading zero) — only after the noon hour do they differ by 12. (The 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is the separate boundary case, written 00:xx.)

If a learner says midnight is 24:00, ask what the clock shows one minute before and one minute after midnight; show that a standard digital clock rolls from 23:59 to 00:00, so midnight at the start of a new day is written 00:00.

When they correctly state 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' (with the noon hour as the exception, both reading 12), reinforce by asking them to predict the next afternoon time before moving the marker.
activities.rationale: Grounding the rule in the structure of the day — a 24-hour span starting at midnight with hours counting on past noon — turns a memorised +12/-12 into a visible relationship and directly targets the +10 error and the 24:00/0:43 boundary traps. A moving marker with paired displays makes the noon crossing observable; a hand-drawn day-line with paired written times is a concrete alternative when no interactive display is available.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: Move a marker along a day-line running from midnight 00:00 through noon 12:00 and back to midnight, watching a 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) readout and a 24-hour readout change together as the marker moves.

Stop the marker just before noon and just after: just before, both displays read 11:59 (11:59 a.m. and 11:59); at noon both read 12:00 and only the 12-hour LABEL flips from a.m. to p.m. (so it shows 12:00 p.m., not 1:00). Then move on past 1 p.m. and watch the 24-hour clock tick to 13:00 while the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. — this is where the 12-of-difference first appears.
Stop at midnight and read both displays; confirm the 24-hour clock shows 00:00 (a new day starting), not 24:00, by looking at what it shows one minute before and one minute after.

For a chosen afternoon time from 1 p.m. onward, read the 12-hour value, then the 24-hour value, and state the relationship: 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' — noting that the 12:xx noon hour is the exception, where both forms still read 12.

If a day-line is available, use its paired displays and boundary labels at 00:00 (midnight, new day) and 12:00 (noon); if not, draw the day-line on paper, mark 00:00, 12:00 and 24:00->00:00, and write both forms side by side for several times.
activities.intendedInsight: The +12 / -12 relationship is not an arbitrary rule but the afternoon and evening hours continuing to count on past 12; noon and midnight are fixed boundaries, the 12:xx noon hour still reads 12 in both forms, and the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 straight to 00:00.

activities.title: Decide before-or-after-noon first, then convert
feedback: If a learner writes 9:45 a.m. as 21:45, stop at the first step: is this before or after noon? Morning times from 1 a.m. to 11:59 a.m. keep their hour, and a single-digit hour gains a leading zero, so 9:45 a.m. is 09:45.
If a learner writes 6 p.m. as 16:00, they added 10: count on from noon 12 -> 13 -> 14 -> 15 -> 16 -> 17 -> 18, so 6 p.m. is 18:00.
If a learner gives 12:43 as 0:43 p.m., note that 12:xx is already afternoon and stays 12:43 p.m.; only subtract 12 from 13:00 or later.
If a learner gives 19:30 as 9:30, they subtracted 10 instead of 12: 19 - 12 = 7, so it is 7:30 p.m.; if they wrote 7:30 with no label, remind them to mark a.m./p.m.
If a learner writes 6:38 instead of 06:38, remind them a 24-hour time always has four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero.
activities.rationale: A worked set covering exactly the discriminating cases (an a.m. time, the 12:xx noon hour, a midnight/noon item, and a single-digit hour) separates learners who reason 'decide before/after noon, then +/-12' from those who just +/-12 the hour. Practising the before/after-noon decision first prevents indiscriminate rule application; formatting the leading zero is rehearsed as a convention distinct from the conversion arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Children tend to treat the hour and minute of a time separately and apply whole-number reasoning to each, which is consistent with mis-applying the +12 rule to the hours alone (including to a.m. times) without reasoning about whether the time is before or after noon.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: For each time given, first state whether it is before noon (a.m.), after noon (p.m.), or a boundary (midnight/noon), BEFORE doing any arithmetic.
Convert 3:45 p.m. to 24-hour time (expected 15:45, add 12) and 9:45 a.m. to 24-hour time (expected 09:45 — add a leading zero, do NOT add 12).
Convert 19:30 to 12-hour time (expected 7:30 p.m., subtract 12) and 12:20 to 12-hour time (expected 12:20 p.m. — stays the same, do NOT subtract).
Write midnight and noon in 24-hour time (midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00).
Write a single-digit-hour time such as 6:38 a.m. in 24-hour form and check it has exactly four digits (06:38).
Always label a.m. or p.m. when writing a 12-hour answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether to add or subtract 12 depends on deciding first if the time is before or after noon; a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 keep their hour (single-digit hours gain a leading zero), p.m. times from 1:00 get +12, 24-hour times from 13:00 get -12, and the 12:xx noon hour, the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (written 00:xx) and the midnight/noon boundaries are exceptions handled by inspection, not arithmetic.

activities.title: Match and build a conversion table
feedback: If a learner matches 6 p.m. to 16:00, have them count on from 12 to find the afternoon hour; 16:00 is only 4 hours past noon, i.e. 4 p.m.
If a learner matches midnight to 24:00, remind them the new day starts at 00:00 and a standard digital clock shows 00:00 at midnight, not 24:00.

When a learner explains 'the minutes are identical and only the hour changes, by 12, from 1 p.m. onward (with the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour written 00:xx)', confirm this is the key idea linking the two forms.
If a learner cannot place a converted time on the analogue clock, link the hour and minute values back to the clock hands before continuing.
activities.rationale: Pairing times across formats and asking 'what is the same, what is different?' builds the relationship rather than isolated answers, and a forced choice against a well-chosen wrong option makes the +10 and 24:00 errors into discriminating decisions. Matching and choosing confirm whether a learner can recognise correct conversions; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct conversions unaided, so pair them with the independent-conversion activity above.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Match a mixed set of 12-hour times (with a.m./p.m.) to their 24-hour equivalents, including at least one morning time, one 12:xx p.m. time, and a midnight item.
Build or complete a two-column table pairing each 12-hour time with its 24-hour form, filling the missing cell in whichever direction is blank.

For a pair you matched, state in words what is the same and what is different between the two forms (same minutes; hour differs by 12 from 1 p.m. onward and in the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour, which is written 00:xx; 24-hour has four digits).

Choose correctly between a tempting wrong answer and the right one, e.g. for '6 p.m. in 24-hour time' decide between 16:00 (a +10 slip) and 18:00, and for midnight decide between 24:00 and 00:00, explaining why the wrong one is wrong.
Represent one converted time on an analogue clock to connect the notation to the clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the two notations paired across many times — and articulating what stays the same (minutes) and what changes (the hour, from 1 p.m. onward, plus the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour becoming 00:xx) — consolidates the rule and exposes the specific slips (+10, adding 12 to a.m., 24:00, dropping a.m./p.m.).

activities.title: Timetable word problems that force the right decision
feedback: If a learner converts a morning timetable time by adding 12, return to the before/after-noon check before the arithmetic.
If a learner gives a 24-hour timetable time back in 12-hour form without a.m./p.m., ask which part of the day it is so the label is included.
Praise answers that state the before/after-noon decision and the reason for adding, subtracting or leaving the hour unchanged, not just the final number.
activities.rationale: Embedding conversions in timetable contexts rehearses the skill where it is actually used and keeps the decision explicit. Word problems can practise and check application but do not let a learner watch the conversion method unfold step by step, so they complement rather than replace the day-line and independent-conversion work.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Read short timetable or schedule problems (e.g. a train leaves at 15:45 — what time is that in the afternoon? A film starts at 9:45 a.m. — write its 24-hour time) and convert as needed to answer.
For each problem, say whether the time is before or after noon before converting, then give the answer in the format the question asks for, labelling a.m./p.m. when giving 12-hour times.
Include at least one morning time, one noon-hour (12:xx) time, and one midnight/noon reference so the morning and noon traps appear in context.
Explain your answer to a partner or in writing, justifying why you added, subtracted, or left the hour unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: The conversion rule is applied to solve real timetable questions, and the before/after-noon check and the boundary exceptions still govern whether to add, subtract, or leave the hour alone.

constraints: Target age roughly 8-9 (Year 4); procedural measurement objective: read, write and convert between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks.

Always decide before/after noon FIRST; add 12 only to p.m. times 1:00-11:59, subtract 12 only from 24-hour times 13:00 onward. a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 are NOT given +12 — they keep their hour, with a leading zero only for single-digit hours (9:45 a.m. -> 09:45, but 10:15 a.m. -> 10:15); the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is written 00:xx.

The 12:xx noon hour stays 12:xx p.m. — do not subtract 12 from it; noon is 12:00 and midnight is 00:00, never 24:00. At noon both forms read 12:00; the 24-hour ticks to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. only when passing 1 p.m., so the 12-of-difference begins after the noon hour, not at noon.
24-hour times always show four digits; single-digit hours take a leading zero (09:45, 06:38).
Always label a.m./p.m. on a 12-hour answer.

Matching and multiple-choice recognition confirm a learner can identify correct conversions but do not by themselves show the learner can construct conversions unaided; pair them with activities requiring the learner to produce conversions in both directions.

A static paired-clock poster can label the two formats but cannot show the marker crossing noon or the boundary behaviour; treat a drawn or printed day-line as a static scaffold and have the learner reason through the noon/midnight transitions aloud.
An interactive day-line is one helpful representation, not the only way to teach this; a hand-drawn day-line, a conversion table, and analogue-clock work are valid concrete alternatives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support general teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6 p.m. = 18:00 (count on from 12: 13,14,15,16,17,18); the +10 slip gives 16:00 which is 4 p.m. — kept 16:00 only as a labelled wrong-answer distractor, never as a correct option. 3:45 p.m. = 15:45; 9:45 a.m. = 09:45; 19:30 = 7:30 p.m.; 12:20 stays 12:20 p.m.; 12:43 stays 12:43 p.m.; midnight = 00:00; noon = 12:00. All verified consistent.

Corrected the noon-crossing description inherited from the original design note/recommendation ('crossing noon ... the 24-hour ticks on to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00'): at noon both displays read 12:00 and only the label flips to p.m.; the 24-hour reaches 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. one hour later. The original wording conflated the noon crossing with the 1 p.m. crossing and contradicted the lesson's own 12:xx-stays-12:xx rule.

Scoped activity[0].feedback[0] to the morning hours 1 a.m.-11 a.m. and named the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (e.g. 12:30 a.m. = 00:30) as a separate boundary case, since the unscoped 'morning hours match' claim fails at the midnight hour. No task in these activities presents a 12:xx a.m. time; only midnight = 00:00 is exercised.

The source labels converting-notation as 'not a spatial task; 3D adds nothing'. This is a catalog-fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted. No claim is made that any single medium is uniquely necessary.

The source framed the day-line marker as the moment the rule 'becomes something seen, not a rule to memorise' and rated it uniquely 'ideal'. This has been softened to one helpful representation among several, with a non-interactive drawn alternative provided, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

'You wrote 6:38 as a 24-hour time — how many digits should a 24-hour time have?'
'12:43 in 24-hour time — is that just before or just after noon? So what is the 12-hour time?'
'If midnight is 00:00, what does the clock show one minute before? Is there ever a 24:00?' (boundary counterexample)

responseLevels.full: Converts both directions reliably — adds 12 only to p.m., subtracts 12 only from 13:00 onwards, uses four-digit leading zeros, labels a.m./p.m., and handles midnight (00:00) and noon (12:00).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set conversions in BOTH directions and WATCH the method: (1) 'Write 3:45 p.m. as a 24-hour time', then 'Write 9:45 a.m. as a 24-hour time.' (2) 'Read 19:30 — what is that in 12-hour time?', then 'What about 12:20?' (3) 'How do you write midnight, and noon, in 24-hour time?' Watch whether they add exactly 12 to p.m. (but not a.m.), use a leading zero, subtract 12 only from 13:00 onwards, keep a.m./p.m. on the answer, and handle midnight and noon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The a.m. item (9:45 a.m.) catches a child who adds 12 to everything; the 12:20 item catches subtracting 12 from noon-hour times; the midnight/noon item catches 24:00. A child whose rule is 'decide before or after noon, then +/-12' handles all three; a child whose rule is 'just +/-12 the hours' fails exactly these.

topic.name: Elapsed time problems
topic.description: Solve word problems involving elapsed time by adding and subtracting time intervals in minutes, including using a number line
evidence: A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?
Calculate how many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05
Use a number line to show the elapsed time between two events
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts football practice at 3:20 p.m. and it lasts 75 minutes, can they work out what time it finishes — using a number line to help?

pedagogy.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — find the END time given a start and a duration, and find the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line. They count on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, whole hours, then minutes). The persistent errors are treating time as base-10 (adding minutes past 60 without rolling the hour), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.
bestPractices: Use a blank number line for both problem types; count on in jumps (next o'clock, whole hours, minutes)
Decide the direction first: adding a duration forwards vs finding the gap between two times
Bridge the o'clock rather than subtracting in columns
Represent the story on the line before calculating (start, jumps, end)
Check the answer against a clock face
keyRepresentations: Blank number line with labelled jumps
Clocks marking start and end
The 'bridge to the next o'clock' jump
commonMisconceptions: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
Column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
Counts in the wrong direction (subtracts a duration instead of adding, or vice versa)
Overshoots or undershoots the o'clock bridge (base-10 slip)

learn.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — finding the END time from a start and a duration, and finding the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line and counting on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then minutes). The core teaching move is showing that the SAME number line solves both 'when does it end?' and 'how long is it?', so elapsed time becomes one count-on method rather than two mysterious sums. Persistent errors to target: treating time as base-10 by writing minutes past 60 without rolling the hour over (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.

activities.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
feedback: If a learner writes an end time with 60 or more minutes (e.g. '2:62' or '3:75'), ask: 'Can a time have 62 minutes? What happens at 60?' Then bridge to the next o'clock first (2:15 -> 3:00) and add the rest.
If the first jump overshoots or undershoots the o'clock, ask 'How many minutes from 2:15 to the next whole hour?' before adding the remaining minutes.
Confirm success by checking: 3:40 + 35 = jump +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15, with the hour correctly rolled over.
activities.rationale: A blank number line lets children bridge to the next o'clock rather than add minutes past 60, directly addressing the base-10 slip. Research documents that children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate its base-60 groupings, which produces minutes-past-60 errors; a published scheme of learning uses the blank number line with jumps to whole hours and minutes for exactly this purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a word problem such as: 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?'
Draw a blank number line and mark the start time (2:15).
Make a first jump that bridges to the next o'clock: +45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Make a second jump with the remaining minutes: +2 to reach 3:02; label each jump and read off the end time.
Repeat with a harder bridge: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Jump +20 to 4:00, then +15 to reach 4:15.
Check the end time on a clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a duration means counting FORWARD from the start; bridging to the next o'clock first makes the hour roll over correctly, so you never write an impossible time like 2:62 or 3:75.

activities.title: Fill the gap to find a duration
feedback: If a learner sets out 10:05 minus 9:20 in columns and borrows in base-10, show that this fails across the hour boundary; model counting on in jumps to the o'clock then the minutes instead.
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 together, ask 'Are you finding how LONG it is or adding two moments? Which jumps fill the gap?'
Reinforce that the two jumps (+40 then +5) sum to the answer the same way the end-time jumps did.
activities.rationale: Modelling a duration as a filled gap counteracts the column-subtraction error that fails across the hour boundary, which a published scheme of learning explicitly warns about, and which research links to base-10 reasoning applied to base-60 time.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a problem such as: 'How many minutes are there between 9:20 and 10:05?'
On a blank number line, mark both times (9:20 and 10:05).
Jump from the earlier time to the next o'clock: +40 minutes to reach 10:00.
Jump the remaining minutes: +5 to reach 10:05.
Add the jumps together (40 + 5) to get the total duration of 45 minutes.
Check against a clock face, and explain why adding 9:20 and 10:05 together would be nonsense.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a duration means filling the GAP between two times with jumps and summing them — not subtracting in columns and not adding the two clock times together. Bridging the o'clock keeps the base-60 boundary correct.

activities.title: Decide the direction before you jump
feedback: If a learner counts backward on a 'find the end' problem, or forward on a 'find the start', pause and re-ask: 'Is the unknown an end time, a start time, or how long it lasted? Which way do the jumps go?'
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 when asked for a gap, restate that a gap is filled with jumps between the two times, never a sum of the clock readings.
Praise correct identification of the unknown and direction before any arithmetic begins.
activities.rationale: Explicitly rehearsing whether the unknown is an end time, start time, or duration addresses the directional/performance error where children subtract a duration that should be added, or add two clock times. Using the one number line for all three cases shows elapsed time as a single jump-counting method, counting forward or backward and bridging the o'clock.
learnerActions: Before calculating any problem, state out loud whether the unknown is an END time (jump forward from the start by the duration), a START time (jump backward from the end by the duration) or a GAP (fill the space between two given times).
Solve a mixed set, e.g. 'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' by counting BACKWARD: -5 to 10:00, then -40 to 9:20.
Compare a forward problem and a backward problem side by side, labelling which way the jumps go.
Say which number is unknown and which direction the jumps travel before marking the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the direction first — forward to find an end, backward to find a start, or filling the gap to find a duration — prevents counting the wrong way or adding two clock times together.

constraints: Pupils should already read and record time in seconds, minutes and hours and compare durations before tackling these word problems; if they write times with 60+ minutes, revisit how 60 minutes rolls the hour over before continuing.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items about elapsed time can check whether answers are correct, but they do not show whether the child built the jumps or bridged the o'clock; pair them with a 'show your jumps' task so the method is visible.
A fixed worked-example diagram can illustrate the jumps but does not let the child build them in either direction; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
A spoken or dialogue format can pose word problems and prompt reasoning, but still needs the child to actually draw and label jumps so the method is practised, not just discussed.

An interactive number line where jumps are dragged and a clock rolls over as each jump lands can make the hour roll-over visible in real time; this is one helpful presentation, not a requirement — the same learning can happen with pencil-and-paper number lines and a physical clock face.
Always state the known times explicitly (the start time for end-time problems, both times for duration problems, and the end time for start-time problems) so the direction of counting is unambiguous.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing and a static image/conversation as unable to let the child build jumps. These catalog-style comparative claims have been softened into scoped notes about affordances and limits rather than universal pedagogical laws.

Arithmetic self-check: 2:15 + 47 min = +45 to 3:00 then +2 = 3:02 (correct); 3:40 + 35 = +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15 (correct); 9:20 to 10:05 = +40 then +5 = 45 min (correct); backward 10:05 − 45 = −5 to 10:00 then −40 = 9:20 (correct). The erroneous learner outputs '2:62' and '3:75' are retained only as misconceptions to diagnose and correct, never as valid answers.
The original row listed a prerequisite reteach id for base-60/hour-crossing; that internal identifier has been dropped in favour of the plain-language prerequisite stated in constraints.

The 'decide the direction' activity targets a performance error (wrong-direction counting) that had no directly supporting source claim in the original row, so its sourceClaims is left empty; the number-line method itself is sourced on the first two activities.

pedagogy.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours to/from minutes, minutes to/from seconds, years to/from months, weeks to/from days — including mixed quantities (3 hours 25 minutes = 3x60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The method is MULTIPLICATIVE (x60, x7, x12), using known number facts, and must resist the base-10 pull that assumes 100 seconds in a minute. The documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, and irregular groupings (months vary in length; a month is not exactly 4 weeks).
bestPractices: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (x60, x7, x12), not repeated addition
Convert mixed quantities in two parts: whole units x rate, then add the remainder (3x60 + 25)
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute, not 100
Handle the reverse (150 s -> 2 min 30 s) by dividing and expressing the remainder
Flag irregular units — months vary; about 4 weeks in a month is approximate, not exact
keyRepresentations: Conversion tables (Days-Weeks, Years-Months, Minutes-Seconds)
The x60 / x7 / x12 rate as a known-fact chain (36 ÷ 6 = 6, so 360 s = 6 min)
A number track for counting leap years / weeks
A bar model splitting a mixed quantity into whole units + remainder
commonMisconceptions: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
Assumes base-10 (100 seconds in a minute, 100 minutes in an hour)
Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
Converts a mixed quantity by ignoring the remainder or the second unit

learn.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days — including mixed quantities (e.g. 3 hours 25 minutes = 3×60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The core idea is MULTIPLICATIVE conversion (×60, ×7, ×12) using known number facts, and resisting the base-10 pull that wrongly assumes 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour. Reverse conversions require dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s). Documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, mishandling the remainder/second unit in mixed quantities, and treating every month as exactly 4 weeks.

activities.title: Multiply-then-combine with a conversion machine
feedback: If a learner gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, ask where the 25 minutes went; have them add the remainder back: 180 + 25 = 205. A bar model separating the whole units (3 × 60 = 180) from the remainder (25) can make the two-part split visible when the leftover is dropped.
If a learner reads 150 seconds as '1.5 minutes', group the seconds into sixties: two complete sixties and 30 left, so 2 minutes 30 seconds — 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30.
If a learner answers '2 minutes' for 150 seconds, point to the 30 seconds still unaccounted for and ask what happens to them.
If a learner uses ×100 for hours→minutes, contrast their answer with grouping into sixties so the 60-grouping is visibly correct.
activities.rationale: A visible multiply-then-add computation with a reverse divide-with-remainder makes the multiplicative structure and base-60 grouping concrete, directly confronting the additive and base-10 errors documented for this topic; the bar model scaffolds the whole-units-plus-remainder split.

learnerActions: Take a mixed quantity such as 3 hours 25 minutes and convert it: multiply the whole units by the rate (3 × 60 = 180 minutes), then add the remaining 25 to get 205 minutes.
State out loud whether you counted up or multiplied, and why multiplying is faster.
Work a reverse conversion: take 150 seconds, group it into sixties — two full groups of 60 make 2 minutes, with 30 seconds left over, giving '2 minutes 30 seconds'.
Test the tempting '100 to a minute' idea against grouping real seconds into sixties, and describe what goes wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting units of time is multiply (by the fixed rate) then combine the remainder — not counting up — and for seconds, minutes and hours the grouping is 60, not 100.

activities.title: Known-facts conversion with a base-10 trap item
feedback: For '1.5 minutes', re-ground on 60: 1.5 of 60 would be 90 seconds, not 150; 150 seconds is 2 minutes 30 seconds.
For '2 minutes', ask about the leftover 30 seconds.
For 8 weeks 3 days, confirm 8 × 7 = 56 then add the 3 loose days for 59.
activities.rationale: Targeted items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options can help surface which error a learner is making (base-10 vs dropping the remainder vs additive). Such items check and may provoke reasoning; use them alongside worked construction, since choosing an answer does not by itself show the learner can carry out the method independently.

feedback: If a learner converts months to days as ×28 or calls a month exactly 4 weeks, use the calendar to show months of 28, 30 and 31 days and distinguish the approximate month fact from the exact week-to-day fact.
activities.rationale: Addressing month-length variability with a concrete calendar directly targets the documented 'every month is exactly 4 weeks' misconception while keeping exact rates distinct from approximate ones.

State why 'about 4 weeks in a month' is an approximation, not an exact conversion.
Contrast the exact fact (1 week = 7 days) with the approximate month fact, and explain how you would convert months to days versus weeks to days.

feedback: Ask the learner to justify their chosen rate; if they add rather than multiply, prompt them to build the ×rate from a known fact.
Probe the remainder: 'Did you keep the leftover part, and where did it go in your answer?'
activities.rationale: Spoken or written word problems let a learner verbalise the method, which may expose additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning. On its own a spoken dialogue does not record whether the learner multiplied or added, so pair it with written working.

constraints: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (×60, ×7, ×12), not repeated addition; for mixed quantities convert whole units × rate, then add or keep the remainder.
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, not 100; the 100-to-a-minute idea should be shown wrong against real grouping, not merely stated wrong.
Handle reverse conversions by dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s), not rounding or dropping the leftover.
Keep exact rates (1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months) distinct from the approximate month-to-weeks relationship; month lengths vary from 28 to 31 days.

Choosing a correct option in a matching or selection item checks reasoning but does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the method; include tasks where the learner carries out and shows the conversion.
A fixed conversion poster or table can display the rates but does not let the learner compute and see the remainder form; treat it as a reference scaffold rather than the main activity.
A bar model (whole units + remainder) and a number track for counting weeks/leap years are optional representations that can scaffold the split and the counting, not required mechanisms.
Illustrative interactions (feeding units into a ×rate step, grouping seconds into sixties, a toggle offering the base-10 reading) are ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic in the source was checked and is correct: 3 × 60 + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 → 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 × 7 + 3 = 59 days; 1.5 minutes = 90 seconds (so reading 150 s as '1.5 minutes' is genuinely wrong, as intended).

The source probe 'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours?' is a base-10 trap counterexample; the correct answer is that 90 minutes = 1.5 hours (since 60 minutes = 1 hour), not 1.9 hours. Retained only as a discussion prompt note, never as a learner answer option; any feedback must state 1.5 hours.

The original keyRepresentation 'number track for counting leap years / weeks' is retained as an optional scaffold in constraints and may be built into a dedicated activity where counting weeks or leap years is practised.

The source's assertions that '3D adds nothing' and that a static image or dialogue 'can't' teach the computation are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative efficacy or necessity of any single format is not established by the sources provided.

The sourceClaims on Activities 2 and 4 support the conversion content, the 'express answers appropriately' convention, and the documented errors, but do not validate the efficacy of selection/distractor items or spoken word problems; efficacy wording is kept conditional.
